Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege.
I wish to lodge an official complaint and request an investigation by yourself or by the RCMP through your office, Mr. Speaker, regarding a postal delivery occurrence originating from this local post office.
Last Saturday, the editor of the West Quebec Post, a weekly paper in the Wakefield area, Mr. Ernie Mahoney, called my home to inform me that 21 parcels with post frank on them, containing information on the proposed goods and services tax, were found in a ditch in the Farrellton area which is near Wakefield, Quebec. These were found by a local farmer by the name of Connor Plunkett.
Mr. Mahoney, the editor, with the help of the farmer returned 20 of the 21 packages to the Wakefield post office. These parcels all bore, as I said, the post mark and addresses in the Navan-Orleans district in Ontario, in the opposite direction.
I find the situation, of course, unacceptable and obviously a criminal act. I would appreciate if you would investigate. I will be forwarding to you a letter with the details.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-20, an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act, be read the third time and passed.
He said: Bill C-20 implements the changes announced in the Budget of April 27, 1989, concerning the federal sales tax and excise taxes and duties. These measures are an important component of the fiscal plan established by our Government to deal with the problem of our substantial and increasing national debt.
During the past four years, Mr. Speaker, this government has made considerable progress in reducing the annual deficit and slowing down the growth of the public debt. Additional measures are needed, however, if we are to sustain economic growth in this country and maintain the programs valued by Canadians. The fiscal plan we presented in the budget will achieve both goals, by reducing spending and increasing revenues. The proposed measures were carefully chosen to ensure a balanced approach that imposes the heaviest burden on those who are most able to bear it. Additional revenues will be drawn from a broad range of sources, including personal and corporate income tax and sales and excise taxes. Meeting the challenge posed by the debt by reducing spending and increasing revenues is a responsibility that we have to present and future generations of Canadians.
In view of the serious financial problems we are facing and in order to spread the burden of controlling the public debt as broadly as possible, this bill implements a number of increases in the federal sales tax. These increases include a 1 per cent increase in the federal sales tax rate on construction materials, from 8 to 9 per cent, effective January 1, 1990. The sales tax on alcohol and tobacco products will be increased from 18 to 19 per cent, effective April 28, 1989. The general sales tax rate is increased by 1.5 per cent, from 12 to 13.5 per cent, as of June 1, 1989. Taxes on telecommunications services and on programming services provided by telecommunications lines are also raised by 1 per cent, from 10 to 11 per cent, as of June 1, 1989.
These measures will contribute nearly $1 billion in 1989 and $2 billion in 1990 to deficit reduction.
Mr. Speaker, in the February 1986 Budget, this Government established the refundable sales tax credit to help Canadians of modest means. To offset the effect of increased federal sales tax rates on low-income individuals and families, the Bill to amend the Income Ihx Act will considerably increase the refundable sales tax credit both in 1989 and in 1990. The sales tax credit for adults will be raised from $70 to $100 in 1989 and $140 in 1990. For children under 19, it will go from $35 to $50 in 1989 and $70 in 1990. Furthermore, the income cutoff for the credit will be raised from $16,000 to $18,000 in 1990 so that more Canadians can claim the credit.
This bill also increases some excise taxes and duties imposed under the Excise Thx Act and the Excise Act. The excise tax on unleaded gasoline is raised one cent a litre as of April 28, 1989 and the excise tax on leaded gasoline two cents a litre. An additional increase of one cent a litre will take effect on January 1, 1990.
Excise taxes and duties on tobacco products are increased substantially by $4 a carton for cigarettes and proportionally for cigars. The duties and taxes on manufactured tobacco products are increased by $5.30 a 200-gram container in two stages to generate revenue and reduce the difference in tax between cigarettes and fine-cut tobacco.
These changes to the excise taxes and duties will bring in some $0.9 billion in additional revenue in 1989 and $1.6 billion in 1990. Furthermore, they meet Canadians' concerns about the environment and dangers to health and tie in with the Government's overall strategy to reduce smoking in Canada.

This bill provides tax relief for Canadians. The sales tax portion of the fuel tax rebate program for primary producers is being extended one additional year. This program provides rebates of federal sales and excise taxes on motor vehicle fuels to primary producers in respect of fuels they use for off highway production purposes.

The program was introduced in the fall of 1984 as a temporary measure and is scheduled to expire at the end of this year. While the rebates of excise taxes will be allowed to expire as scheduled, the sales tax rebates are being extended to December 31, 1990.
A new sales tax exemption is being introduced for machinery and apparatus purchased for use in the processing or treatment of toxic wastes in toxic waste treatment plants. This measure will respond to Canadians' concerns about the environment by reducing the cost of equipment acquired by toxic waste treatment plants to process toxic wastes in Canada.
This bill also implements several minor technical amendments to the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act. A number of amendments to this bill were proposed by some hon. members at report stage. Most of the proposed amendments related to the deleting of various clauses of the bill.
Interestingly, some of the motions would have deleted measures that would reduce taxes, such as clause 4 which extends the sales tax portion of the fuel tax rebate program for one additional year and clause 7 which provides a new exemption for machinery and apparatus for use in the treatment of toxic wastes.
On the other hand, some interesting proposals were made in the course of the debate on the merits of using the tax system to further the government's environmental objectives. While the House did not adopt any of these motions, hon. members may be assured that I have noted their comments on these issues.
This is an important bill. It will raise substantial additional revenues and implement a significant part of our plan to deal with the serious problem posed by the public debt. By reducing annual deficits and controlling the debt, we will be able to maintain the valued social programs and high standard of living Canadians have come to expect for themselves and for their children.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to reply to the hon. minister's address on this bill, Bill C-20. As a Canadian I would like to think that this government was interested in the finances of this country, but its entire record since taking office has indicated that it could not
Government Orders
care less either about the welfare of this country or the welfare of Canadians.
The minister is trying to tell us that through some enlightenment he is now concerned with reducing the deficit.
When this government came to power there was a $22.6 billion interest tab on the debt that existed in this country. At the present time the interest on the deficit amounts to over $39 billion per year. The interest alone on the debt has increased by over $17 billion per year.
The government is now talking deficit because the election is behind it. It wants Canadians to believe that it is concerned about the economy of this country, that it is concerned about the welfare of Canadians. I find this deception of the government very difficult to accept.
The facts indicate that this is a government that callously and without concern for the people of this country has followed its own agenda. It has the people of Canada to look after themselves. It has an agenda that is going to open up our trade with the United States and link its interests with big business. The Tories say: "If in the meantime we act in your welfare it is coincidental and we wish you all the luck in the world".
This bill is nothing more than a preview to the gross deception that is yet to come, and that is the goods and services tax. A former friend of the government calls it "the gouge and squeeze tax". This bill is just a preliminary step to keep the pump primed until this government can get the big dollars. That is what it wants.
How can Canadians possibly believe that this government wants that money for any other reason than to squander it on what it considers its friends would like to have and on what will be in its best political interest?
Canadians will not accept that this government is interested in the welfare of this country or in the welfare of Canadians until it cleans its own house, until it deals with the management of this country in a way that Canadians feel is not only prudent but absolutely necessary. Until this government does something about bringing about government, bringing back political will to Canada, the country and its people will never accept tax increases in the nature that this government is putting forward.

October 23, 1989
Government Orders
We are asked to accept these increases in the federal sales tax and the excise tax. This is not the first time we have been asked to accept tax increases by this government. It is not the second time. It is not the third time. It is the fourth time that this government has come to the people of Canada and stated that it wants to increase the sales taxes and the excise taxes. This is the same form of consumption taxes that the Prime Minister himself "called the silent killer of jobs". In this case, the Prime Minister might ultimately be correct because if this government follows through with a goods and services tax, then there will be a silent killing of jobs and a noisy reaction from the people of Canada.
This is not going to be acceptable no matter how much this government tries to advertise and to make Canadians think that this is all in their best interests. We Canadians are no longer surprised to see such hypocritical action and double talk on the part of the government. The government is not going to deceive Canadians into believing that the goods and services tax, and these constant taxes, one after the other, time after time, are going to be in their best interests.
What are we going to get when we get the goods and services tax? We now have excise tax on gasoline at 13.5 per cent, the maximum, as if it were machinery manufactured in Canada. We have the sales tax at 13.5 per cent. We have the excise tax now at 8.5 cents a litre for non-leaded gasoline and 9.5 cents a litre for leaded gasoline. These taxes are tremendously high. Is this government going to take them off when the goods and services tax comes in? No, the government is not going to remove them. What it will probably do is tell Canadians that we need an environmental tax. We have to look after the environment.
The minister is talking about this tax as being an environmental tax for what we have to do for the environment. The environment is tremendously important. I just wish that the government realized how important it is. Canadians do, certainly on this side of this House we do. We only wish the government did. But the government will realize it, or at least it will in its pronouncements when it feels it has to issue a new tax. In addition to the goods and services tax we will undoubtedly be dealing with an increase in the sales tax and the excise tax in gasoline to justify keeping that tax where it is at the present time.
This government has a history of double talk. We have seen broken promises in other areas. We have seen it with VIA Rail. This government has said that it would improve rail services in this country and would never create second-class citizens. Well we have seen what has happened to that promise. The government has slashed rail services in this country and the people in the Atlantic and the north and in certain parts of western Canada are certainly second-class citizens in the minds of this government.
Everybody's favourite line is when the Right Hon. Prime Minister told voters: "Social programs were a sacred trust never to be tampered with". Canadians have come to realize that there is nothing sacred to this government, nothing at all.
Why, time after time after time, have we as Canadians, not only been misled, but have had the intelligence of everyone in this country insulted by the misleading policies and the misleading pronouncements of this government?
I would like to just go over this GST and talk about the inconsistencies with respect to what this government has said the goods and services tax would do and what this tax will actually do.
On October 8, 1988, during the election campaign, the hon. Minister of Finance said: "The bottom line is that the sales tax will not be used to raise the revenues of the Government of Canada". The reality is that the revenue is going to be used to raise the revenues of the Government of Canada. The revenue from the present tax is going to be increased from $18.5 billion to $24 billion. At the same time that the government is saying it is not going to raise revenues with the new sales tax, the revenues of the new sales tax are going to be used to fight the deficit. Now, if you do not have new revenues how are you going to fight the deficit? And even if you believed the government were interested in fighting the deficit, that record.
Second, the technical paper on the GST says that the GST will improve the over-all fairness of the tax system, that lower and modest income Canadians will be better off once the GST is in place. How can that be when the Standing Committee on Finance, at its hearings across the country, has literally had welfare groups and social interest groups from one coast to the other denounce it as being a flagrant tax grab that will position than they are today?
October 23, 1989

Even the Deputy Minister of Finance admitted that many low and middle income Canadians will be worse off when the GST is put into place. That is from a deputy minister. How can we ever believe that this government was actually concerned about the welfare of low and middle income Canadians?
In another segment of gallantry, the Minister of Finance also promised that: "Sales tax reform will eliminate the hidden tax in the prices consumers pay". But again, reality stands in the way of believing the words of the minister. The government is going to allow these retailers to state whether the tax is to be included in the price or is going to be added separately when the item is purchased. The government cannot have it both ways. It cannot say it is not going to be a hidden tax and then, at the same time, leave it to business to determine whether it is going to be a hidden tax or not.
These are the things we were told before election day. We were told this so that it would not become an issue, so that the government could feather out this whole question of the sales tax to make it palatable for Canadians so they would not ask questions. Whenever a question was asked the government came out with an answer that it thought we, in the Liberal Party, or Canadians wanted to hear, not the truth. That was not the important thing. It was getting through the election campaign and telling people what they wanted to hear. Then, once the election was over, sock it to them.

Good-bye Charlie Brown is right.
Another infamous document, the White Paper on sales tax reform states: "A good sales tax should not impose heavy compliance costs on business or create undue administrative costs for government". Well, what have we seen? What we have seen is that small businesses are going to be devastated by the cost of complying with this tax. We are going to impose upon small business a tremendous tax. We are going to impose on business in this country a $2 billion cost to comply with this goods and services tax. The president of the Federation of Independent Business, a former friend of the government, is now saying that the allowance that this government is going to pay to small business is not going to come close to compensating small business for the cost of having to comply with this tax. But this government is saying: "Well, that is the only thing we can do. The present 13.5 per cent tax on manufacturing is not working. We have to find an alternative and this is the only alternative." This is what is being forced down the throats of Canadians. It is unacceptable. If it were true, it

would be unacceptable. The tax we have now is certainly better than the one this government is going to gouge from the Canadian people.
How do we know that this government has done its homework? Every indication seems to indicate that it has not. The Minister of Finance will stand in his place and say: "We tried to get it worked in with the provincial sales tax, but the provinces would not agree". I am afraid that the Canadian people have taken a poor second place to the government's determination to maintain its honeymoon, such as it is, with the provinces.
Can you, Mr. Speaker, just picture the Minister of Finance saying to his provincial counterparts: "We do not have to impose the GST. Why do we not work together and try to work it all into one national sales program? You do the collecting and we will split the revenues," and the provinces saying: "Stick it in your ear". Then the Minister of Finance says: "Oh, well, I tried". That would be end of the dialogue.
That is the determination that this government has tried to work on developing a national sales tax. What do we have? We have this complete and utterly unworkable situation, gouging the Canadian people, costing small businesses millions and billions of dollars to try to implement and put it into place, not to mention the additional public servants that we are going to need to bring it about and enforce it.
The government, by its own admission, says there are going to be over 2,500 new public servants. That is only what the government admits. We know from experience what the government admits we can multiply by quite another number. It is not acceptable by any stretch of the imagination.
I think it is time, and I think that Canadians feel it is time, that the job of the opposition, and certainly of the Canadian people, is to remind the government of what it is supposed to be doing, to remind the government that it made commitments prior to the election; that it has obligations that it has to honour; to remind the Prime Minister that the mark of good government, Mr. Speaker, is not how well you cozy up to big business, but how you represent the people of this country. It is a challenge to this government of restoring decency, honesty and integrity to government. For this government, that is going to be one heck of a big job. But the sooner it does it, then the sooner we are going to be able to get this country back into the profile we want it to be, the profile it used to have.

Government Orders
Right now the government is going in the other direction. It is taking all of its time, and all of the money it can get its hands on, to convince Canadians that they should want something that they do not want. The government has spent $20 million on an ad campaign to try to force down the throats of Canadians the acceptability of the goods and services tax. Canadians have listened. Canadians have heard. Canadians are repulsed by what their own government is trying to do. The Canadian people will not accept the line of advertising and the line of "hoi polloi" and hocus-pocus that this government is putting forward.
This is not going to be another free trade debate. The Canadian people now know what the free trade arrangement has meant to this country. They now know that they cannot believe what this government wants them to believe.
Let us make no mistake, Canadians from sea to sea, regardless of economic status, background, party affiliation or ideology, reject this tax completely and utterly.
In just the few short months since the technical paper on the goods and services tax was released thousands of petitions have been signed and registered. There have been letters to the editors in all of our national newspapers. Members of Parliament of all political affiliations have received hundreds of letters in total, denouncing this goods and services tax and the protests are not diminishing. We have heard the petitions today. We have heard the voice of Canadians. It says: "Don't implement this goods and services tax. It is not acceptable". Canadians are fed up with being taxed to death while this government squanders the money that being paid in taxes on things that are in its own political interest and to the advantage of its own political cronies. We saw this during the last e lection campaign with the money for ACOA a five-year program, almost all spent in the election campaign. Not one year's worth of funds spent, not two, but three, four, maybe even five years' funding
spent in an election campaign to try to buy the votes of Atlantic Canadians. Well, we saw what happened.
This government is misreading Canadians. Canadians want fair government. They want good government from their representatives. They do not want to be told and convinced of something they do not want. When they tell the government they do not want something, they do not want this government to yet again try to convince them that it is in their best interests and what a wonderful thing it its.
In the history of this country there have been few proposals that have received such massive opposition as has this GST proposal. It is overwhelming as a member of Parliament to speak to people. In a recent poll it was determined that 80 per cent of Canadians are opposed to this tax. Yet, the government forges on, trying to convince Canadians of what a wonderful thing it would be. It is trying to cut a hole through a wall of water and the government is going to be oblivious to the torrential downpour that is going to come down on top of it.
This is yet another case of this government not listening, not wanting to listen to the people of Canada. It is a completely, utterly flagrant abuse of democracy. We have the Prime Minister and the Deputy Prime Minister stating that they have something that they want to force Canadians to accept, but 26 million people or 80 per cent of the 26 million are saying no. A few members in the government are saying yes, and to them that is the democratic process that they are going to force down the throats of Canadians. They expect Canadians to say one morning when they wake up: "My goodness, I was wrong all along about the GST. What a wonderful thing it is".
Well, Mr. Speaker, if you believe that that is going to happen, then there is a bridge in Brooklyn I will sell to you at a very reasonable price. The opposition to the GST will not collapse. It has not even begun to waver. Canadians refuse to be coerced into accepting something that they do not feel is in their best interests or is even going to do what this government says its is going to do. This is in spite of the millions that is being spent to try to force this upon Canadians.
October 23, 1989

The manufacturers' sales tax as it exists right now at 13.5 per cent, as the government would say, is the only alternative. It is not the only alternative.
The people of Canada feel that the government has not managed the country properly and they are not going to accept this completely oppressive and obscene tax, knowing that the Government of Canada has no conception in its own mind of how to manage the economy.
What this government wants to achieve through this advertising campaign is a great example of what George Orwell in his novel 1984 put forward when he talked about double speak, which was the tool of big brother. Once again we have double speak by the Minister of Finance and by the Prime Minister. Just last month we saw double speak in action, in a way that I think big brother would have been very proud.
The Minister of Finance on Monday, September 25, introduced new terminology to the English language. He spoke of the goods and services tax as being a "fairness package" and having "fairness features". If it wasn't so pathetic, it would almost be funny.
The Minister of Finance referred to the goods and services tax as a "fairness feature". Doesn't that sort of makes you warm and tingly all over, to think that our government is going to put forward a fairness feature. Perhaps what he means is that Canadians will not suffer abject poverty. If Canadians do not really suffer abject poverty, are not completely down and out, then this taxis fair. If he leaves them with a few loonies in their pockets, then this tax is fair.
That is not what Canadians think is fair. In fact, even with the minister's fairness feature, which is his tax credit, 300,000 families living at the poverty level right now are going to be worse off. That is his fairness feature. Sure, he is going to give a few dollars back to the people, but only a portion of what he is taking away from Canadians, who can least afford to lose this money. The reality is the fairness feature tax credit that the Minister of Finance is going to give back will still require an average family of four, two parents, two children, with an income totalling $45,000 a year to pay $629 more in each tax year.

The minister referred as well to the fairness feature tax credit for business to help them recover the cost. I have already referred to what small business thinks of that. As I stated earlier, this fairness feature is just going to give small business back a portion of the amount that they are going to have to pay to collect this tax.
Canada will be the only country in the world with two different sales taxes, a sales tax provincially and a sales tax federally. Imagine the complications that this is going to cause to small businesses.
Why then, in view of the problems that this tax is going to create, is this government constantly subjecting the people of Canada to psychological manipulation? Why is it trying to force this down the throats of Canadians? We have seen the saga of the Standing Committee on Finance, led by that redoubtable crusader, the chairman, flying across the country speaking with Canadians, insulting them one by one as he goes, leaving a trail of bad feelings and complete disgust everywhere he lands.
It was the dubious privilege of the Atlantic provinces, just a few days ago, to have this caped crusader in their midst, the Batman of politics. He landed in Newfoundland and when witnesses came before him he kept saying: "Hurry up, hurry up, I have got to catch a plane. I cannot listen to all of this". He did not tell them, of course, that the plane was at his disposal and the plane would only go when he said it could go. He was pushing Canadians. He had allowed two days for the four Atlantic provinces on an issue as important as this. He was not even going to hear from the tourist industry of Nova Scotia. He still did not hear testimony from the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, an organization that represents 8,000 businesses in Atlantic Canada. This is the Batman that we talk about. I am telling you that this Batman may be fortunate to be able to hang from the ceiling of a cave by his feet when the people of Canada go looking for him.
This is insulting to the people of Canada. Yet, why is this being done? Why is all this attention being directed to our fearless crusader who is going across Canada and to the Minister of Finance? I suppose the more attention that we can attract to these fellows, then the more heat is taken off the Prime Minister. What a wonderful ploy.
If we were to look at the last five years of this government, we would find it very difficult to sum up exactly where it has gone because it has been like a balloon flying through the air with the air coming out of it. It has been zigzagging all over the place helter-skelter.

Government Orders
We cannot look at this government as having any concern for Canadians. We cannot give it a tag which says that this is a government that really is interested in the people of Canada. We cannot do that because it is not true. We cannot say it is the government of the depression years or the war years. Probably the best tag we could give this government would be related to the $1 piece that it brought out and call them the "loonie years". That is really what it amounts to.
There is nothing in this government for the people of Canada other than abuse and absolute misleading policies, redundancy, and absolute abandonment of principles. Why? Because this government is interested in following the course of the United States, marching in lockstep with the government of the U.S. as if it really believed that it knew where it was going or even where the Government of the United States was going.
I think it is interesting to read the October 23 edition of Time magazine. The cover story relating it to the American government states: "Is Government Dead?" There is a little caption saying: "Unwilling to lead, politicians are letting America slip into paralysis". This is what we are following?
Is it not evident that this is exactly what we are following? Before it is too late, we must start to pull this country together, to develop a financial package and a financial program that is going to help this country, not to completely and forever take Canadians into the wilderness and try to convince them of something that every Canadian knows is not helpful and is not true.
Before it is too late, will this government do something decent for this country? Will it do something decent for Canadians? Will it be honourable enough to develop policies that are going to help Canadians and not try to destroy this country?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the New Democrats, I want to join the opposition to this bill which is really a product of the
budget, and reflects so much what was in the budget material, and follows the pattern set by the Conservatives ever since they were first elected in 1984.
Certainly the trend was established before that. It was bad enough before, this continuing process of loading more and more of the cost of maintaining government services in Canada upon the lowest income people, upon the middle income people, and relieving those at the top of the heap from paying their fair share. It was bad enough before 1984, but the process has certainly accelerated in every budget since the Conservatives produced their first budget after the 1984 election.
Their whole thrust, it would seem, has been to get revenue out of the people's pockets by adding on to consumer taxes of one kind or another. The estimate that we have produced is that up until this budget they have taken an extra $900 in tax from the average Canadian family between the years 1984 and 1988 through sales and excise taxes alone. It is part of the pattern that existed before but has been increased since to get more and more of the government's revenue from such taxes.
The increase in the sales tax on construction materials, equipment and building materials from 8 per cent to 9 per cent is an increase in the rate of tax of 12.5 per cent. That begins January 1,1990. The increase in the sales tax on alcoholic beverages and tobacco products from 18 per cent to 19 per cent begins on April 28. An increase in the sales tax on telecommunications and programming services from 10 per cent to 11 per cent begins June 1, 1989, another increase of 10 per cent. There has been an increase in the sales tax on all other goods to which it applies from 12 per cent to 13.5 per cent, the manufacturers' sales tax. That is an increase of 15 per cent in the rate of tax.
This is the tax that other members and the Minister of Finance himself have referred to as the silent killer of jobs. It would seem as though the minister felt that he has done enough to kill jobs in Ontario, so he is increasing the rate of taxation alone by 15 per cent and making all the rest of the country pay the cost of his attempts to keep the lid on what is happening in southern Ontario.
October 23, 1989

Our estimate is that in this one budget alone the increases in sales and excise taxes is going to add another $500 per family on to the $700 that the Conservatives have already levied against every average Canadian family.
Consumption taxes are unfair. I think everyone will agree with that. Even the government will lend some measure of agreement to the idea that taxes should be based on the ability to pay and should not simply be a general sales tax.
There are other methods. We have talked about them during the budget debate. We have talked about other methods the government could have used to increase its revenue, if increasing its revenue was the main aim of the government in the first budget after the election campaign. We mentioned several of them. I mentioned several of them myself.
There is still some 50,000 profitable Canadian corporations that will be paying no tax even under this budget. There are very wealthy, high income individuals who because of the various allowable tax expenditures will pay no tax in spite of the increases. There is no point putting a surtax on an income tax if the individual is paying no income tax to start with.
I am not opposed to the idea of putting a surtax on the income of wealthy individuals, but I am opposed to them not paying the tax in the first place, the tax upon which the surtax can be levied. To talk about making it fairer by bringing in a further tax on consumption, the goods and services tax of course is the greatest misleading statement of all.
The increase in the federal services tax from 3 per cent to 5 per cent I cannot find too upsetting. It is another personal tax increase, and we have always argued that it should be based on the person's ability to pay. People who are paying that kind of income tax can pay the other surtax.
An additional 3 per cent for individuals with incomes over $70,000 will begin July 1. When you add that to what is already there, that will mean they will be paying an 8 per cent surtax. Those are the people who can afford to pay more revenue to the government.
On the other hand, when we look at the pattern of what the government has done, we realize that in the five-year history of the government it has reduced the maximum tax for people with incomes over $100,000 by $3,500 and, even after putting this increase into effect, those people will still be paying less income tax than they
Government Orders
were when the Conservatives were first elected. It is obviously unfair.
It is part of the process of putting the weight more and more on the lowest income and on the middle income people and of continuing to provide relief to those with the highest incomes. They have done nothing to close the loopholes that exist for the 6,250 individuals in the highest income tax brackets who have not been hit by this government, indeed who have been relieved.
Other legislation is before the House that I might just refer to briefly. The shift from general revenue to premiums for regionally extended UI benefits adds another $1.7 billion tax on payrolls. For individuals with maximum insurable earnings this will mean a direct tax hike of about $90. It is another way of loading the cost of government upon the lowest and middle income people so that it will not be necessary to hit those at the highest levels.
A large corporations tax is to be levied on corporate capital in excess of $10 million, creditable against the existing 3 per cent federal surtax on corporate income. At least it is getting something, but we have to realize that this is not a minimum tax on corporations. Like the capital tax on banks, it taxes assets, not profits, and it will only apply to 3,600 corporations leaving tens of thousands still not paying corporate tax.
Speaking of banks, I recall the concern expressed by the banks or at least by the people who were buying bank shares before the last budget. They expected the government to come in with a new tax on banks and trust companies. Unfortunately that did not happen and the price of bank and trust company shares went up markedly in the market the next day. They were expecting to be paying some $4.1 billion-that was the finance minister's own figures-but it did not happen. His explanation was that it was going to be too difficult to administer. So easy to get more money out of the people at the bottom of the heap, so difficult to administer some new tax that is going to hit the wealthiest of all corporations in Canada. I wonder why it was so difficult.
They took a little bit off the corporations. They hit a few of them. They go to the bottom again and they hit small business. There is an increase in the effective small business tax rate from 12.4 per cent to 12.8 per cent and an increase in interest charges for overdue income tax payments of individuals by 2 per cent, which is simply following the increase in the prime rate that perhaps has had the greatest effect on the budget. Without that the deficit this year could have been substantially lower than it was the year before.

October 23, 1989
Government Orders
I recall that during the election campaign we expected the deficit to be $28.9 billion and then we found out when the budget came down that the latest figure was $35.5 billion, an increase of $6.7 billion in what the deficit was expected to be. It was totally attributable to the increase in interest rates and there would have been a substantial reduction had interest rates not increased so much.
They are passing some of that on to the people who are behind in their income tax instalments. Still, there is nothing to go after the $36.1 billion in deferred income taxes corporations have been allowed to postpone. As some of them say, they do not expect ever to pay it and, as some have argued, we cannot really collect that because it is never going to be paid. Yet, the corporations are able to claim this, to report it.
We could at least-I have argued this before as have others on our side of the House-charge interest on that deferred corporation tax. As long as it is sitting there on the balance sheets, let the Conservatives get some interest from it and let them get it at the same rate as they are getting it from individuals at the bottom of the heap. But I do not expect that to happen. That is contrary to the direction in which the government has been going since it was elected some five years ago.
According to the National Council on Welfare, sales and excise taxes have been the predominant source of new tax revenues since the Conservatives came to office, reflecting a 55.5 per cent increase in the revenue from those sources. The contrast is that revenue from personal income taxes increased by 33 per cent since 1984 and from corporate income tax by 17.7 per cent, not that the rates have gone up but rather that there had been that much more money or inflation. That is why the amount has increased.
The government should have followed up on what it was saying. It should have tried to make the tax system fairer. A more appropriate target, rather than going after the people at the bottom of the heap, would have been to have gone after the $30 billion patchwork of tax credits that are allowed to individuals and corporations.
The government then comes up with this proposal of bringing in a new tax system that is supposed to be fairer, the goods and services tax, and once again, going after the people at the bottom of the heap. I know that what I have said on this subject previously has been quoted in the House and has come back to me. I think that some of it bears repeating from my mouth as opposed to coming from somebody else's.
The goods and services tax, as it now stands, is not a fair way of getting more money from the Canadian public. We should be going to the individuals and corporations that have it, that can afford it, that are earning the incomes and are not paying tax at an appropriate rate.
There was a proposal which came out some 22 or 23 years ago in a report that was three years and a couple of months in the making, the Carter report. The report had good proposals for making the tax system fairer. As a matter of fact, the proposals were going to be so good for the people in the low and middle income brackets and so fair for the ones at the top that neither the Liberal nor the Conservative governments paid any attention to that report since. The Conservatives might well go back and look at that, if they want to be fair, to see whether there should not be for the first time in the history of Canada a truly fair system of getting revenue for government services.
The goods and services tax is not fair. The lower the income, the higher proportion of income one will pay in this tax. The government says we are going to mitigate that by having a system of credits, but we are going to make sure that we keep getting more money out of the lowest income people because that tax credit is not going to be fully indexed, only partially.
That way year by year, while the people in the lowest income brackets are getting credits paid to them, nevertheless they will have them clawed back each year through the government's failure to fully index these payments.
There is another way. I have spoken of this before and I am going to try it again. The government said that it was really going to be great, that it was going to give the credit every three months. It was not going to make us wait until the end of the year. Mr. Speaker, I do not know if you have any people in your riding who are on welfare, or whether you have ever had any experience with this, whether you have ever known anybody in that circumstance, but they are operating on a pretty tight budget. To have to wait for three months to recover the money that they spent on the first day after they got the previous cheque is asking a bit much of them.
October 23, 1989

A lot of single parents with very low incomes, raising families, trying to educate them, are going to be asked to somehow or other budget so that three months from the latest one they will get another cheque from the government to reimburse them for the cost of paying the GST. They are getting other payments every month. Is it that difficult to pay them monthly rather than quarterly?
I am not speaking in favour of the system. I am still opposed to the fact that it is not fully indexed, but there ought to be a way of getting those cheques into the hands of the consumers who need them so desperately more frequently than once every quarter. I hope that plea will not fall on deaf ears. I do not suppose we really know the answer to what the government is going to do about groceries. On the face of it at the moment it looks as though the most exotic of foods, if you buy them in a grocery store, will be tax-free. I hope I do not offend anybody, but if you buy the lowly hamburger in a fast food outlet you pay tax on it. Now it is the lowly hamburger that provides so many meals for families that cannot afford anything else. In some cases it is cheaper to buy that hamburger in a fast food outlet than it is to prepare it at home, though the quality would be a lot better at home. Nevertheless it is more economical. Those foods are taxed the way the system is now while the most exotic of foods bought in a grocery store will not be taxed. That is not fair.
People who have the means and are close enough to the border to drive across and load up with groceries will not be paying any tax on anything they bring in that way. If you cannot get across the border and have to buy goods in a store on this side-I am not talking now about groceries; I am talking about all goods generally-then you pay tax. That is not fair. There has to be a better way of handling it.
I recall reading a story when I was in the Victoria legislature written by someone in Montreal who was talking about various stock markets across Canada. Does anybody in the Vancouver exchange have a hope of making a profit? The average investor has better odds of making a profit if he bought Lotto Canada tickets. Yet
Government Orders
that is tax-free. You can play that kind of gambling where a lot of money changes hands by the people who can afford it and pay no taxes, but if your mother goes out and plays bingo for an evening she pays taxes. That is not fair. If one form of gambling is going to be taxable then the other should be as well. Indeed it should be the other way around if anything.
The GST is supposed to be visible. Well it is like taxing the banks. It is difficult so we abandoned that idea. Anything that the government does not want to do, it says it is too difficult. If it means that the people at the bottom of the heap will know how much tax they are paying as compared to those at the top who do not really care, then it is difficult because the government does not really want to do it. The government does not really want them to see a cash register tape which identifies the amount of their income that is going to that tax. It is too difficult so it will not be done.
It is supposed to be revenue neutral. As we read the material that has come out recently we see that some $5.5 billion will be available for deficit reduction. Well that is not fair. It is not intended to be fair. We said from the beginning that it was intended that this would help reduce the government's deficit. It is so much easier to do it by taking more money from the people at the lowest and middle income brackets through this goods and services tax than it is to reduce the interest rate.
Then of course labour is supposed to carry the brunt of it. Its members are supposed to be the good people. They are supposed to say: "We know it is in the interest of government as a whole. We recognize we are paying more than our share, but we are not going to ask for any increase in wages to make up for this shortfall". It is not fair to go to that group in our community and say it has to pay the cost of the government's mismanagement of finances.
There are better ways of getting more income from the people who can afford it. The government should abandon this excise tax bill and come back with a proper plan that will get a higher proportion of its revenue from those who are best able to afford it.

Mr. Speaker, I think we have all heard stories of various groups coming before the finance committee and talking about the expected effect of this goods and services tax on their communities. Financing it and the structure of the organizations that are doing it all cost more the farther you get away from the centre. The 9 per cent is applied to that total so the GST will be even more unfair with respect to the people who live farther away from the centre of activity than it will be here in Ottawa or Toronto.

From my point of view the biggest thing the government could do would be to reduce the interest rate. It would affect not just the cost of interest, but it would also get the economy moving in other parts of the country. It would reduce the costs of unemployment and make a bigger contribution to our economy if the government could just bring itself to forget about the free trade deal to the extent of letting our interest rates drop, at least down to the point where they were some years ago when there was just a four point spread between us and the United States.

Mr. Speaker, over the past 30 years it seems that the proportion of the tax burden in this country has shifted dramatically. Some 30 years ago, 50 per cent of the burden was paid by corporations, 50 per cent was paid by individuals. It seems that over 30 years of successive Liberal and Tory governments that burden has now shifted to the point where 80 per cent of the tax burden is paid by individuals, much of it through consumption taxes such as the one we are dealing with today, and 20 per cent of taxes are now paid by corporations. There seems to have been a dramatic shift in the direction of forcing the burden of taxes on to individuals in this country.
At the same time there has been a parallel development. Ownership of the Canadian economy has been more and more vested in a very small group of people or a small handful of holding companies. Diane Francis mentioned in her book Who Controls Canada that something like nine families and a small handful of holding companies control 50 per cent of the assets on the Toronto Stock Exchange, so the economy is very tightly held. Even El Salvador is owned by 14 families. Canada's economy is even more tightly held than the economy of El Salvador.
I am wondering if the member can suggest to us ways in which, by redistributing the tax burden in this country, we can also redistribute the ownership and democratize the ownership of our economy so that more Canadians can feel that they own our economy and have a democratic interest in the directions that our economy is going. Flas the member any suggestions in that direction?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel very privileged to be able to stand here this morning and speak on Bill C-20. This bill contains the legislative amendments required to implement the federal sales tax and excise and duty changes announced in the budget.
This government proposes a 9 per cent goods and services sales tax to replace what it deems to be a regressive and economic liability to Canada in the 13 per cent federal sales tax. The federal sales tax was 9 per cent when this government took over in 1984. If it was so hurtful to our economy, why was it increased from 9 per cent to 10 per cent, to 11 per cent, to 12 per cent, and now to its present 13 per cent? It does not make sense. The Prime Minister called it a silent killer of jobs, yet he went ahead and increased this silent killer of jobs.
The government's opening speaker this morning commented on how this tax will help reduce the deficit. Is this something new we have been hearing recently? When it was originally proposed, there was no mention that this goods and services tax would help reduce the deficit until a few people, other than those on the government side, started checking into it and suddenly realized that there were billions of dollars in excess revenue over what was required from the FST that would be earned. So the government finally had to admit that it was not revenue neutral. I guess Canadians are saying, "Can this government ever make up its mind?"
We all went through an election in the fall of 1988. Unfortunately, nothing was mentioned except free trade. There was no mention at all that this country was faced with the largest deficit it has had in its history, that from 1944 to 1988 that deficit had doubled in size. There was no mention of this at all by the government. Yet here we are now into the Thirty-fourth Parliament, and all of a sudden the government is finally coming clean and saying that there is a serious problem with regard to the deficit and that we must reduce it.
I think that all of us as concerned Canadians are interested in reducing this deficit. But in 1991, if this goods and services tax goes ahead as planned by the federal government, Canadians will pay a new tax whenever they make purchases from a wide range of goods and services. The new sales tax, for most Canadians, will be applied in addition to the existing provincial retail sales tax, especially here in Ontario-I guess in all provinces except Alberta-with which they are now so familiar.

October 23, 1989
Government Orders
The proposed GST will also be a new experience for businesses. Today some businesses collect and remit retail sales tax, while those which produce or import manufactured goods collect and remit the federal manufacturers' sales tax. There are still, however, numerous enterprises which never see the current taxes directly because they never sell nor buy taxed products at the retail level, nor do they produce or import manufactured goods. This tax would then dramatically affect the way in which sales tax revenue is collected at the federal level.
The GST, as outlined in the August technical paper, is predicted to generate $24 billion in 1991, this amount being based on the rate of 9 per cent. Of this total revenue, about $18.5 billion would replace the revenue lost by the elimination of the existing MST, which by 1991 would have been levied at a rate of 13.5 per cent for most products. The remaining $5.5 billion would be returned to taxpayers in one form or another. By far the most important element in this regard would be the greatly enhanced sales tax credits. The existing system of credits would have cost $1.2 billion in 1991, and the proposed credits would cost about $3.6 billion. The difference of $2.4 billion was be financed by GST revenues. Finally, about $2 billion in revenues would be transferred to individuals and provinces as a result of the GST's impact on the price level.
The introduction of the GST is expected to raise prices by about 2.25 per cent. The remaining $200 million in GST revenues is slated to pay for additional administrative costs which include hiring at least 4,000 people to administer the GST.
There are many arguments both for and against. As the most recent poll has indicated, 80 per cent of Canadians say that there are more reasons against than for initiating this GST. As I stated earlier, all Canadians are concerned about our deficit and all Canadians will gladly find measures to reduce that deficit, but this is not the way to go. This is what they are saying. They are saying it in spades, and I think it is high time that we started listening.
The argument against revenue neutrality is further strengthened by noting that the federal government, in proposing a reform of the sales tax, has recognized the serious problem associated with the erosion of the MST base. The 13.5 per cent MST rate might well be viewed as untenable over time. Rather, it is only a temporary measure until such time as the GST can be put in place.
Tax expenditures are increasingly being substituted for program expenditures and loose interpretation of the concept of revenue neutrality allows tax base measures to be unnoticed in a way that expenditure measures could not be. By stressing the alleged revenue neutrality in the tax reform, the government is pointing out that there are structural problems inherent in the present tax system which need to be addressed. But these are two distinct issues and, unfortunately, the government is confusing them.
Let us look at the case of two sets of adults living together, one couple married and one couple living common law. The married couple would be entitled to a maximum GST credit of $550 which would be reduced on the basis of family income. Each individual of the couple would be entitled to an adult credit reduced on the basis of individual income. Rather than having the credits start to diminish at $24,800 of total income, as in the case of a married couple, their credits might not start to diminish until total income reached $49,600 if both adults earned the same amount.
In addition, the unmarried couple would be treated as single individuals. The common law couple would then be entitled to two tax credits. In other words, members of this House, it is far more beneficial tax-wise to live together as an unmarried couple than it is to live together as husband and wife. Now I think that is disgraceful.
We know there will be an impact on housing and, undoubtedly, housing accounts for the single largest expenditure made by families. This is true whether one rents or whether one buys. The GST would impose a 9 per cent tax rate on the retail price of a new house purchased from a developer. Thus, the GST has the potential to increase the price of new houses substantially. To offset this impact the government is proposing to rebate up to one-half the GST otherwise owing, subject to restrictions on the price of a house.

Government Orders
Clearly the tax implications of the shift to a GST would vary across Canada since house prices vaiy greatly. As the technical paper notes, home buyers in Toronto would face the greatest adverse effect of this change. The imposition of the GST on new housing would then raise house prices and confer a windfall profit on owners of existing housing.
On rental accommodation, in 1991 or later all aspects of the construction of a building would be subject to the GST, as would the cost of the land. Long-term residential rentals would be exempt from the GST. No tax would be collected on these rents and the landlord could not claim an input tax on any GST paid.
The introduction of a new and larger tax on new construction should raise rents across the land. As the tax drove up the prices of new apartments, some demand would shift to old apartments. But an increased demand for older apartments could not increase the fixed supply, obviously so the consequence would be fully reflected in price hikes in that market also.
The GST is a value-added tax rather than a sales tax. A sales tax can be thought of as a tax on a transaction rather than a tax on a product. Thus a provincial sales tax might be applied to a product numerous times. Think of an automobile which is sold new and taxed and later resold through a dealer and taxed again. This kind of multiple taxation should not occur with a GST type of value-added tax.
Why then would used products be taxed under the GST? There are several reasons. Used goods compete with new products and are often sold by the same retailer. If one were taxed and not the other, compliance costs for the seller might increase and an opportunity for tax evasion might present itself. Thxing one and not the other might also distort the relative prices of the two types of goods, especially if an untaxed source of used goods, say through imports, were available. As, well the sale of used goods often involves the creation of some value-added, and by taxing this sale that value-added can effectively be taxed. It is confusing stuff. I do not know who the heck is going to understand and know what to tax and what not to tax.
Last week I spoke on the GST and how it would affect municipalities. It is going to have a very, very grave effect on them. I will not go into this again. The municipalities have only one way of raising taxes, namely, through the property tax. What this government is doing is looking for revenue from municipal government, a government that is not able to raise its revenues. And yet, this government wishes to make gains on the backs of a municipal government.
In conclusion, the provinces are almost faced with a fait accompli. Ottawa plans to introduce unilaterally a sales tax of 9 per cent. It is obviously going to have a serious effect on provinces because there is already a sales tax in all of them except Alberta. The provinces would have to bear the full weight of resentment toward a tax of between 9 and 18 per cent. But even more important for the provinces, their refusing to participate in this sales tax leaves the federal government on its own to carry the borrowing of the money.
The intent of the goods and services tax is to provide the federal government with an efficient alternative, so it says, to the MST. Efficiency would be achieved by taking a fairly broad base, thereby minimizing distortions and consumer choice. By crediting the tax paid on business inputs, the GST is also intended to remove from capital and thus enhance productivity. I do not think it is going to do any of these things. It is going to have one of the most deleterious effects on the economy of this country. We know it is going to raise the inflation rate. We know it is going to raise the interest rate. We know there is going to be a slow-down in business. Why, oh why, is this government insisting on it? Eighty per cent of Canadians say "stop" say "no". For goodness sake, let's listen to them.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member on her speech and on her grasp of the subject of the goods and services tax. She has really done her homework and understands the problems involved.
I think it is somewhat ironic that today we should be talking about tax increases and this particular tax, when this is the first day of Small Business Week in Canada. My question is directed to the Hon. Member, who I know has many small businesses in her riding, and I

October 23, 1989
Government Orders
wonder whether she could tell the House about the attitude of small businesses in her riding. What does small business think of the new GST, the new tax on goods and services? I think everyone in this House agrees it will be an administrative nightmare.
Mr. Speaker, with your permission, I would like to hear what the Hon. Member has to say about small businesses in her riding.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for the question. One of the things that I have done in my riding is to try to analyze the business community's attitude toward the GST. I did that by circulating a copy of the government's pamphlet on the GST to every business in my riding. I, in turn, also circulated the Liberal response, the opposition party's response, to the government's proposed goods and services tax. This way I was providing them with both sides of the spectrum, the government's side and the opposition's side. I was not trying to influence the business people, I was allowing them to make up their own minds with the information presented.
I also asked that if they felt, as we on this side of the House feel, that it was going to hurt business, would they sign a petition which I would be pleased to present in the House of Commons. These petitions are coming in on a daily basis. The small business community in the riding of Nepean is very, very concerned about the business tax.
There is not enough rebate being allowed to small business. The paperwork is going to be horrendous. The costs are going to be horrendous but much more important the community is telling me that business will suffer, and suffer badly. People see a definite downturn and I feel quite confident in standing here this morning and saying that I am speaking for the majority of the small business people in the riding of Nepean in that they do not wish to see this GST imposed upon them. They cannot afford it. Many have told me that they will literally be forced out of business.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget on which this particular Bill C-20 is based is an illegitimate budget to start with in that it gave advantage to people across the country who are in the privileged position of knowing what was in this budget before it was presented to the
House of Commons. Consequently, people had opportunities. We do not know much about that. Therefore, we should consider Bill C-20 an illegitimate bill in itself. What it does is increase, as the member put forward, the tax in areas which are already regressive. Would the member give us some indication of how she feels the direction is impacting on her particular constituency?

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are probably several ways in which these will be impacting upon my constituency. I have mentioned the business people. Maybe it was in a previous speech, I forget, but the senior citizens of our country are probably the people who are most concerned and will suffer the greatest with the GST. I have had literally hundreds of calls and hundreds of letters in my offices. Some are from the adult population in Nepean saying that they will not be able to afford it.
One senior said to me "My wife and I have raised a large family. We worked hard. We never took a holiday. We never wanted to leave our children." He had an average income, and told me that they had never bought a new car but bought Canada Savings Bonds because they believed in Canada. They did this consistently for years until their children were grown and through university. Here they are at a stage in their lives-they are both retired-when they can afford to take that holiday south. They can afford to buy that new car. Their income is over the $50,000 range and they are saying to me, "I will sell my Canada Savings Bonds. Why should I keep them? I will sell my Canada Savings Bonds and reduce my income so that my old age security pension cheque is not clawed back." I do not blame those senior citizens. I can guarantee that this government is going to lose billions of dollars through people selling their Canada Savings Bonds or through the non-purchase of new bonds. I think that will have a dreadful effect on all Canadians.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak. I can look into the future. I know you did not know that but that is it.
I see on bookshelves across Canada a story of "the taxingest government in the history of Canada" or maybe a book that is named "the grabbiest government in the history of Canada".
October 23, 1989

This chapter of Bill C-20 is chapter 7 of the grabbiest government in Canada's history. If you look over the last five years of government, you will see that chapter 1 was the initial budget. Actually it was not a budget.
It was a statement by the Minister of Finance, who started the process of increasing the taxes for the people of Canada, reducing the taxes for the corporations of Canada, and developing a system which impacts particularly on those who can least afford to pay taxes.
Chapter 7, Bill C-20, is an act to amend the Excise Tax Act, and an act to amend the Excise Act. It sounds dull and sounds innocuous, but the taxpayers are going to find it a particularly interesting chapter because it amounts to one more tax grab. We have indicated on many occasions that any kind of sales tax, any kind of consumer tax, is a regressive tax. This book that I am speaking of started during those last four years. It started increasing the very taxes that are being increased again today in this particular bill.
I can list for you, Mr. Speaker, if you want to hear them, exactly what each of the tax increases were over those five years. Do you want me to do that, Mr. Speaker?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext: Not particularly.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
I am not sure that I want to do it either. In any event, this chapter is peculiar as well as interesting. As I said a few moments ago, the budget on which the bill is based, is an illegitimate budget. The leak of the budget gave many people in privileged positions information which they could use to their advantage. Never in the history of Canada, in the history of parliamentary governments, has that been allowed. Whenever it is found that somebody had a previous and early look at a budget, the indication was that it should not be passed. Therefore, it would be withdrawn. But not with this government.
The idea of taking advantage of a budget is not acceptable in a parliamentary government. This particular government did not seem to want to remove its budget from the books. It has gone further by bringing in Bill C-20 to further take advantage of not only the lower-income Canadians, but those on welfare and those without any income because the moneys they get will not go as far in keeping them alive.
Government Orders
The arrogance of the government is expressed very succinctly here. We have had no change. Surprisingly, the government made no real attempt to justify the fact that it had allowed people to take advantage, or allowed the situation where people could take advantage, of the budget. It made no effort to justify that. Consequently, we have here an illegitimate budget and an illegitimate bill. But the arrogance of this government is such that we are forced to look at this as if it were a legitimate operation.
Let us have a look at Bill C-20. I live in northern Saskatchewan, and I have spent a considerable amount of my life in northern Canada, places like Inuvik, Whitehorse in the Yukon, and in northern Quebec. I recognize that there is in this particular budget a far-reaching impact that is much greater on remote and northern areas than there is on downtown Toronto or Ottawa, for instance. There are a number of areas in which the taxation in Bill C-20 will have a direct impact upon the people of the Yukon or Northwest Territories. It increases the tax on fuels, on aviation fuel. One of the real differences between the southern part of Canada and the north, and you do not have to go too far north to recognize this difference, is the cost of fuel for travel and for heating. This bill increases the cost of fuel. It increases the cost of fuel by increasing the tax on that fuel. Consequently, it is a tax which is much greater on those northern, remote areas of the country. Transportation costs are greater to get the product to those places and this additional tax has been added to that cost.
Tourism is a major industry in many northern parts of Saskatchewan, Ontario and British Columbia. Tourism is a major industry in all the northern parts of Canada. This tax is going to increase the costs of all of the tourist industry across the country. It is going to increase the costs by increases in the cost of gasoline, fuel for ground transportation as well as air transportation.
It is not as if we did not know the impact of this kind of a tax. Last year, the government put on a communications tax. That is the kind of tax we are looking at now, a communications tax on every long distance telephone call in these areas. If you live in a northern community and you want to talk to your doctor, to your school about your children's progress, or to somebody who is going to supply you with gasoline or parts for whatever your industry happens to be, you are going to call long distance. If you live in Ottawa and you want to do any of these things, not one of those calls will be a long distance call and there will be no tax on them. But if you live in a northern community you will pay 10 per cent on every call that you make for every substantial item that you require to survive. That is an increased tax on northern

October 23, 1989
and remote communities much greater than the 1 per cent increase on gasoline. But it is an increase which is there and it behooves us to look at it. It is the same kind of tax as the GST. It is going to be on all products and it is going to impact on northern communities much more than southern communities.
I will continue after Question Period.
