Mr. Speaker, 33 years ago on October 23, 1956, the flame of freedom briefly burned to light the darkness of Stalinist Hungarian communism.
The freedom fighters were just that, men and women who fought to bring freedom to their beloved homeland. The world watched with bated breath as a handful of patriots dared to challenge the mighty Soviet giant in pursuit of democracy and human rights. Despite promises made, the western world stood by while they fought on valiantly, courageously, heroically, to the death. The blood of these patriots seeped into the ground but was not forgotten.
Now, 33 years later, the tree of democratic reform has begun to bear fruit, thanks to the nourishment it received from those who fought and died in 1956.
Much is happening in Hungary today. Reforms thought impossible only a few years ago are enacted almost daily. We in Canada and the western world watch with hope. But we must also be ever vigilant that the fruits of the sacrifices of the freedom fighters will not be spoiled by renewed repression.

Mr. Speaker, on October 5, the Minister of Employment and Immigration announced that she had lifted the moratorium on deportations of Haitians. She said she believed the political situation in that country had returned to normal since a great wave of violence disrupted the November 8, 1987, attempt to hold elections there. Therefore,50 rejected refugee claimants are to be deported from Canada to Haiti, the first one tomorrow.
For decades, Haitians were terrorized by the Duvalier regime. Since 1986 they have had four successive governments installed by force of arms.
According to the June 1989 Overview on Haiti published by the Immigration and Refugee Documentation Centre, human rights violations continue under the latest regime. These include torture, extrajudicial executions, disappearances, arbitrary arrests and detentions.
The Tontons Macoutes still roam Haiti, possibly sanctioned by the military government.
I call on the minister to read the Immigration and Refugee Boards's report and to talk with Amnesty International before returning Haitians to risk death.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to announce that the National Transportation Agency has today issued Order No. 1989-R-326 apportioning costs for the reconstruction of the overhead bridge crossing the CN lines near Truro, Nova Scotia.
October 23, 1989

This bridge is in a serious state of deterioration and has had its capacity reduced repeatedly to the point where it cannot legally accommodate any more than a light truck. Everyone involved agrees that the bridge must be replaced immediately. The tracks in question divide the community of Salmon River right down the middle and are a barrier for school buses, ambulances and firefighting equipment.
I now call on all the parties involved, including CN, the National Transportation Agency, the province of Nova Scotia and the municipalities to work together to ensure that construction of the new bridge begins immediately and this problem is brought to a logical and safe conclusion.
I commend the National Transportation Agency for its determined efforts which have resulted in this order today.

Mr. Speaker, today is the first day of the week dedicated to small business. The government has selected the following slogan for this occasion: Grow today for tomorrow.
The government's cynicism is truly incredible, Mr. Speaker. It talks about growth for Canadian small businesses, when it is trying to impose a tax on goods and services, the GST, that will be a nightmare for small businesses.

I ask this government to withdraw the GST. That would be the best way to show that it cares for small business, which in the last 10 years has accounted for 93 per cent of the new jobs in the private sector.

Small businesses are the motor of our economy, Mr. Speaker. During the past ten years, small business created 93 per cent of the new jobs in the private sector.
If the Conservative government is anxious to defend the interests of small businesses, it should immediately withdraw its new goods and services tax.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Employment and Immigration has shown her commitment to the riding of Elk Island through the Lamont-Two Hills Community Futures Program. Community Futures is geared to helping workers in communities which have serious economic problems but show potential for growth.
In order to maximize a community's economic potential the program is guided by local board representatives who assess community needs and recommend support for business development, skills training or job relocation.
As part of the program, the Lamont-Two Hills Business Development Centre will receive $400,000 in federal funding to continue assisting small business in the area. During its first year 11 businesses were either started or maintained through the technical and financial services available at the centre. As a result, over 28 full-time and part-time jobs were either created or maintained.
Community Futures is solid evidence that the Government of Canada is committed to our rural communities.

Mr. Speaker, this year's National Universities Week, which ended yesterday, caused Canadians to think about what universities mean to Canada's future and to realize that investment in our universities is at risk.
University classrooms are overcrowded. Professors have less time for individual students and existing research grants are insufficient. Yet advances in science and technology-particularly in medicine, biotechnology and communications-depend on university education and research.
Thus, I welcome the inclusion of education on the agenda of the upcoming First Ministers' Conference, considering that education has not been discussed at these conferences since 1973.

October 23, 1989
However, I am concerned because education will merely be one item among many to be discussed during only half a day of the two-day conference.
A First Ministers' conference should be convened which will focus specifically on the topics of education and research, to adopt a definite commitment to fund them so that we will experience a budget boost in this area instead of a budget blow.

Mr. Speaker, countless Albertans from all walks of life have expressed their concerns to me about the environmental impacts of the proposed pulp mills for northern Alberta. Edmontonians have written letters, telephoned and expressed their concerns directly to me.
The federal government and the province of Alberta have embarked on a joint environmental review. The review panel is presently holding hearings in towns throughout northern Alberta. This forestry investment will have major social, economic and environmental impacts on the whole of Alberta. Yet the review panel will not be holding hearings in Edmonton or Calgary.
All Albertans are subsidizing the forestry projects. All Albertans own the resources of the province. Debate must be encouraged, not discouraged.
I call upon Alberta Environment Minister Ralph Klein and the federal Environment Minister, the member for Lac-Saint-Jean, to ask the review panel to at least hold public hearings in Edmonton. All of Alberta is affected. All Albertans must be heard.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on the occasion of Small Business Week, October 22 to 28, to express the New Democratic Party's recognition of the vital contribution of the small business community to Canada's economic growth and well-being. It is significant to note that in the past 10 years almost 70 per cent of all new jobs have been created by small businesses, many of which have less than five employees.
How ironic that Small Business Week-this celebration of entrepreneurship in Canada-takes place at a time when the continued economic viability of the small business community is under attack by the federal government's proposed goods and services tax. The GST will effectively turn individual small businesses into Revenue Canada tax collectors, forcing small businesses to carry the overwhelming burden of administering this tax. The GST will add to the mountain of paperwork already faced by small businesses and will substantially increase accounting costs.
I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that Small Business Week is an appropriate time for the government to demonstrate its commitment to small business by withdrawing the proposed goods and services tax.

Mr. Speaker, once again, Canada Post wants to terminate the local air service that carries perishable goods to the Inuit and Cree in New Quebec. Although it has not announced its intentions publicly, Canada Post has already increased postal charges by 30 per cent, 45 per cent and even more. The situation will become critical after November 13, 1989, and will have a direct impact on consumers in Northern communities. This is a complex situation which concerns Canada Post, the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs and the Department of National Health and Welfare.
If the government is trying to save money, it is in fact creating more serious problems that will affect the health and well-being of Northern residents. Mr. Speaker, this is another instance of people being unfairly penalized, compared to those living in southern communities.

Mr. Speaker, in a major snow storm on Friday, 36 centimetres of snow fell, paralyzing northern Ontario between Marathon and Sault Ste. Marie for more than 24 hours.

Northern Ontario residents were denied access to any road or air travel. The only transportation system operating for those residents was VIA Rail.
Had this taken place on January 16,1990, the day when the VIA Rail cuts come into effect, the residents of northern Ontario would have been left without any means of transportation whatsoever, and this will happen in this year. This government obviously did not consider the weather of northern Ontario in its decision to eliminate the Canadian and the CP line which services close to 400,000 people.
Friday's storm illustrates all too well that this government has chosen to isolate these communities because of, for lack of a better word, a stupid decision. The people of northern Ontario implore this government to change its mind before it is too late.
Do not stop passenger rail service in northern Ontario, depriving the people in Wawa, White River, Marathon, Terrace Bay, Schreiber, Nipigon, Red Rock, Hurkett, Dorion, McKenzie, Thunder Bay, Ignace, Dryden, Ke-nora and many, many small communities of less than 500 people of passenger rail service because it will be eliminated.

Mr. Speaker, today marks the beginning of Eating Disorder Awareness Week.
The National Eating Disorder Information Centre is working to sensitize Canadians to the serious health hazards associated with such disorders as anorexia nervosa, bulimia and overeating.
Anorexia and bulimia are reaching epidemic proportions across Canada, affecting one in five college women and an increasing number of men. Between 10 and 20 per cent of anorexics die as a result of their eating disorder.
The National Eating Disorder Information Centre and the Bulimia and Anorexia Nervosa Association are working to help Canadians combat the low self-esteem and other psychological, physiological and societal factors that lead to these disorders.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare along with all hon. members supports these organizations in their endeavours and wishes them every success in their education campaign this week.

Mr. Speaker, now the National Capital Commission wishes to establish an eighth official residence in Canada, this newest one for the Chief of Defence Staff.
This proposal comes at a time when the federal government is preaching restraint, at a time when we have thousands of homeless, at a time when our soup kitchens are overflowing. What will be next? Will the Clerk of the Privy Council want a residence? What about the Deputy Minister of Finance, or perhaps even the chair of the National Capital Commission?
We see the government dismantling the national infrastructure with cuts to VIA Rail, the CBC, the privatization of Air Canada and the refusal to aid municipalities in their problems with infrastructure decay. We see this government failing to prepare for the future by drastically cutting back on research and development and weakening environmental legislation.
Yet it seems to think that these things do not matter as much as subsidized housing for the Chief of Defence Staff. For a government that is constantly calling on Canadians to tighten their belts, we never see a sign of it doing this. It seems to have removed its own belt so as to lash out at Canadians. I demand that it put it back on, tighten it and begin to look at important issues affecting all Canadians.

On the first day of the tenth annual Small Business Week in Canada, I want to take this opportunity to salute millions of Canadians who take risks in order to start small businesses.
Mr. Speaker, since 1984, more than 150,000 small businesses have been created each year in Canada, and according to a recent study, more than 65 per cent survived the first three crucial years.

October 23, 1989
Oral Questions
Four Canadians out of ten employed in the private sector work for a small business. In fact, 80 per cent of the new jobs created between 1978 and 1987 were in the small business sector.
Mr. Speaker, these figures spear for themselves and demonstrate the vital role played by small businesses in Canada's economy. The federal Government is aware of this contribution, and that is why it has done more than any other government to help small businesses in the past five years.
Mr. Speaker, this government firmly believes that in Canada, small business is big business.

Mr. Speaker, Saturday's The Globe and Mail displayed a front-page photograph of the Prime Minister and his spouse sitting in a rickshaw. Below the photo was the caption "riding in style". The imagery is an anachronism. It speaks volumes of this government's insensitivity toward the developing world.
Does the Prime Minister know anything about rickshaw drivers and the poverty in which they live? Rickshaw drivers are among the poorest people in the world. The development organization Inter Pares was doing something about the impoverished state of rickshaw drivers. Most drivers must rent the rickshaw from fleet owners at exorbitant prices.
Three years ago Inter Pares set up rural co-operative workshops in Bangladesh to enable them to become self-sufficient. This is what real development means.
The Prime Minister's budget put an end to the Inter Pares project. This Canadian organization is now looking to Europe to continue financing the co-operatives.
It is a sad day indeed when a Canadian organization running a successful program must appeal to other governments to keep development projects alive. I hope the Prime Minister left a big tip. Undoubtedly the driver could use it.

['Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order.\nI wish to advise the House that an agreement could not be reached under the provisions of Standing Order 78(1) and 78(2) with respect to an allocation of time to the report stage and third reading stage of Bill C-21, an act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act and the Employment and Immigration Department and Commission Act.\nUnder the provisions of Standing Order 78(3) I give notice of my intention to move a time allocation motion at the next sitting of the House for the purpose of allocating a specified number of days for consideration and disposal of proceedings at those stages of the bill.']

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
Last week, the minister indicated in this House that the supply of natural gas reserves in this country were so vast that despite the NEB approval to export 9.2 trillion cubic feet we would have no problems for future energy security.
That statement has now been contradicted by a senior official in his own department who said that the minister's comments and assessments were, in fact, academic and meaningless because of the difficulty of developing these resources for economic needs.
Under these circumstances I would like to ask the minister this. Is he prepared now to revise his comment, revise his advice to cabinet and give a commitment in the House today-that the cabinet will not approve the NEB decision until there can be clear evidence provided that this export of natural gas will not endanger the security of energy supply for Canadians?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reference to what I said in the House those figures taken from the Geological Survey of Canada. The 9.2 tcf were placed against the 11.65 tcf of known and proven reserves of up to 56 tcf which was given by the Geological Survey of Canada. In fact, I have been given figures today by the Geological Survey of Canada which puts both numbers even higher.
The issue that we are dealing with is the question of how much of that gas is extractable in deep water conditions as well as northern conditions. That I think can only be determined if and when there is a pipeline application by either a company or a consortium of companies and the conditions that they would place.
What the NEB did with the export licence application last week-on the basis of the reserves that it had proven and the amount asked for on the application-was approve from its perspective an export licence. As I said, the GSC has figures today that could put them even higher than the figures I gave last week.
October 23, 1989

Mr. Speaker, the issue is much simpler than that. It is whether we will be putting at risk the security of energy supply for Canadians. It is the responsibility of the cabinet to make that decision.
I ask the minister specifically, will he commit that before any further development or decisions are taken that the government will provide publicly to this House a clear indication of what the level of reserves are, and that it will not provide any approval of an export licence or permit until it can prove that there is sufficient reserves for Canadians and that they will not be put at any risk by this pipeline application?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the member and I both know that cabinet has to approve the export licence.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: That is the weak link.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
If the Whip is speaking about a weak link, I am sure he lives with it personally every day.
I am saying that cabinet will have to examine the export licence. I say to the Hon. Member that the NEB in its mandate obviously has to take a look at reserves, as well as the applications before it.
I say to the hon. member as well that he should be careful in assessing the matter as he did in his question because it goes back to the National Energy Program. The underlying argument of the National Energy Program was that if it was kept in the ground we were going to maintain reserves, and we were going to maintain the 25 year figure for Canadians in terms of security of gas.
I think all of us recognize that the activity in the oil and gas fields and the reserves are best increased if we allow that activity, which will also allow the cash flow that is needed in order to have further exploration and to have reserves built up.
I guess what I am saying directly to the member is that the plan of the NEP did not increase reserves. It gave a false sense of security about reserves in the future. It did not give us the reserves that we have now.

Mr. Speaker, we are not arguing about the NEP. We are arguing about
Oral Questions
the NEB, and the decision to authorize an export permit which could put energy security at risk.
As the minister clearly knows, because of the free trade agreement any export to the United States-including the 9.2 trillion cubic feet-would increase the level of exports to the United States to close to 60 per cent of our normal reserves.
Does the minister really believe that the best interests of this country are served by locking away in perpetuity 60 per cent of the natural gas energy reserves of this country to another country? Is that really defending the security and best interests of Canadians?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do know what helps with the security of supply. One way is to have activity in the gas and oil fields. A second way is to give a return to those who are doing the exploration. Third, Canadians will have to re-examine in terms of long-term contracts that they have access to that gas.
If the hon. member looks at the export licence that was granted by the NEB, he will note very clearly that the NEB put down conditions whereby before an export contract could be granted to the United States, Canadians would need to have access to that information and to that gas as well. I say to him that I believe the market-place is the best place in which to have this function. It functions best with the NEB putting forward the conditions that it did on the export licence.
The last point that the hon. member should know is this. Before there is going to be any export, it will be based on a pipeline application. Those conditions are going to be raised and caveats obviously will be considered by the NEB to maintain security of supply for Canadians.
He should recognize, as I think all of us do here, that we cannot and should not consider that after the number of years we have been in the frontier we can simply continue having exploration and delineation without finally bringing that gas down and having the cash flow we need.

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Deputy Prime Minister. The Prime Minister has repeatedly said that no major economic initiative will be undertaken until the government has a complete environmental assessment.

October 23, 1989
Oral Questions
Now that the National Energy Board has given preliminary approval to the export of 9.2 trillion cubic feet of natural gas from the Arctic, will the minister guarantee that the Prime Minister's word will be honoured? Will there be a complete public review before the export licence is given approval by Cabinet?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think we have to differentiate again as to what happened. What happened with the NEB was that it had before it an application on an export licence and approved 9.2 trillion cubic feet.
What the hon. member is relating to, I would think more logically, is that when a pipeline application is made and heard by the NEB a full environmental assessment is done, as we have done on every other megaproject, whether in the north or for that matter any other part of Canada. It was done with Hibernia and Lloydminster. It will be done in the north if, first, an application for a pipeline is made and, second, a pipeline application is approved. It is at that stage that the environmental questions, the socio-economic questions, and the land claims questions all come into consideration. They will then have to be discussed and evaluated by the NEB.

Mr. Speaker, this is potentially the largest export of energy in the history of our country. My question is quite simple. Is there going to be an environmental assessment? How is it going to be carried out? I think this issue is important enough for the future of the north and for the future of all Canadians.
Is the government going to take this environmental assessment more seriously than it took the one on VIA Rail? In other words, is the Prime Minister's word going to be honoured this time?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member looks at the record with respect to energy projects, she will find that an environmental review was done on OSLO, Lloydminster and Hibernia. In fact, the point that I make to her is that in every one of those projects, as well as if there is any pipeline bringing gas down from the frontier, there have to be the environmental assessments as well.
The answer to the environmental question is, yes. But I say to her very directly, do not confuse a pipeline or potential pipeline with an export licence.

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Finance about government secrecy.
Last Friday, the minister confirmed that he would not release the 500-odd pages of documents about economic forecasts in 1988, made prior to the election for the year 1989. That answer was just not good enough.
I want to know today from the Minister of Finance why he promised the House of Commons on October 10 that we could have the information when nine days later he was denying the information to the House of Commons. What happened between October 10 and October 20 that made the minister change his mind? Is there all of a sudden some new version, the Wilsonian version of the truth in this country?

Mr. Speaker, nothing changed from October 10 until last Friday. If the hon. member looks back to what I said on October 10, he will see I said that the information that the applicant was entitled to would be released. That is what has been released to the applicant.

Mr. Speaker, it was the party across the way with Walter Baker and Ged Baldwin which was so concerned about openness and secrecy in government many, many years ago.
What I want to know from the minister is this. Since I filed a request for access to information in March for the government's communications plans for its budgets of 1985, 1986, 1987, 1988, and for its plans for the White Paper on Taxation last year I want to know why he turned down that application in June. Why do we still not have that information? Why is he also withholding information on the unemployment insurance cutbacks from this House? I want to know why he is not forthcoming. Why this secrecy? Will he stop playing his silly little games and be open and honest with the people of Canada?

Hear, hear!
Mr. Wilson (Etobicoke Centre) Mr. Speaker, I would have to review the particular reasons and the content of the application for the turndown which was given, as he has referred to, in June. I do not have that information readily at hand.

What we are looking at here is a very important principle of parliamentary responsibility. That is that the minister is responsible for the management of his department. The minister is accountable to Parliament for the management of his department.
Along the course of those activities of managing the department, there will be information and advice provided by the public servants to the minister to allow the minister to do his job, to carry out his responsibilities. Ele is not bound to accept all the advice of deputy ministers, nor is he required to hide behind the advice of deputy ministers. Those decisions have to be made each time decisions are taken. But it is absolutely essential that there be confidentiality of the advice between the deputy minister and the minister so that that free flow of information will continue. It is on that basis that the access to information provides for the confidentiality of that information.

Mr. Speaker, that is just not good enough. We are really seeing a Wilsonian version of the truth, and I can tell you that even Conservative backbenchers are upset with him.
I will give him a third try. The minister, according to his own calculations, said that at least one province will suffer a negative impact under the GST.
I want to know today whether or not the minister will confirm that that province is Alberta, give us the dimensions of the negative impact and, while he is on his feet, tell us whether or not he will release all the documents pertaining to the impact of the goods and services tax on all 10 provinces and both territories in this country?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is quite aware that I have been very open in all the dealings that I have had with Parliament and I will continue to be very open in all the dealings that I have with Parliament.
The hon. member has made reference to the impact of the GST on the provinces. I have commented on that in a general way in this House. I have also said that we do have a tradition in our dealings with the provinces to discuss information with them before we go public with it in order to ensure that the information that is released
Oral Questions
to the public is not misleading. Until we have that discussion with the provinces, no, I am not prepared to make the information available.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance is aware that the vast anti-GST coalition is growing every day. My question for the Minister of Finance is this: Is he prepared to acknowledge today that the government's proposal to tax goods and services has been rejected by people across the country, and is the Minister of Finance prepared to put an end to the confusion of consumers and the uncertainty created in the private sector by withdrawing this terrible tax?

No, Mr. Speaker, I am not prepared to withdraw the goods and services tax. We have put forward a technical paper. The finance committee is hearing comments on that technical paper.
I think the hon. member will agree with me that there is broad agreement that we must move from the existing manufacturers' sales tax, which is deeply hidden in the production process, and move to the goods and services tax. People have disagreements with this. Some say there should be no exemptions and others say there should be exemptions, and many people have said they would like a lower rate, but there is no agreement whatsoever on how to get the rate down. Some say we should reduce the credit while others say the credit is not large enough, it has to be increased. Some say reduce the housing rebate and others say the housing rebate is not large enough.
Clearly, the disagreement with our proposal is on both sides of the proposal. I believe that the package that we have put on the table represents a very carefully constructed balance and a balance that is proving itself as we hear these recommendations from other people.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Minister of Finance.
Speaking about being on the table, the Minister of Finance has insulted his counterparts, the provincial Ministers of Finance of the provinces across this country, by saying they are playing political games with the goods and services tax.

October 23, 1989
Oral Questions
Canadians do not believe for a moment the minister's contention that the provinces rejected a national sales tax proposal. Just to make sure we can make the record very clear on this, my question for the Minister of Finance is the following.
If, in fact, the provinces rejected the government's national sales tax proposal in April, would the minister make public the proposal that was rejected by the provincial Ministers of Finance? Then we will know who is telling the truth in this matter.

Mr. Speaker, we have been working with the provinces since the early part of 1987, discussing all aspects of the goods and services tax. At the stage that we are talking to the provinces, we are talking about a federal-provincial tax which has a large number of the attributes of the goods and services tax that is in the technical paper proposal today.
It became very clear from the comments that have been made in the past week and last August when the premiers met that the provinces do not have any sense of urgency, any real desire to move ahead with a goods and services tax proposal. When we saw that that was the case, and because of the very real sense of urgency that we have as a federal government to move away from an existing tax which is broken and which the finance committee of the House of Commons agreed on two occasions had to be changed, on that basis we felt we should move ahead with a federal only proposal.

Mr. Speaker, recently the Deputy Prime Minister sent a letter to the chairmen of the various House of Commons standing committees referring to the deficit and requesting that the chairmen submit any ideas that they might have on deficit reduction. However, as chairman of the Public Accounts committee, I did not have the honour of receiving such a letter.
Why did the Deputy Prime Minister fail to send a letter to the chairman of the Public Accounts committee? Is he afraid that he might get some constructive suggestions from this committee which, after all, is the
watchdog committee of the spending of this government?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can certainly give the hon. member that assurance. Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance said just a moment ago that it is becoming "very clear" regarding the GST. I agree with him. It is becoming veiy clear every day that middle and low income Canadians will, under the proposed goods and services tax, fall farther and farther behind each year because of the caveat that tax credits will only be increased if Canada's inflation rate is more than three percentage points. Even government members of the finance committee are quoted as recognizing that low and middle income Canadians will be hurt.

Will the minister finally acknowledge the truth and agree the GST will hurt low and middle income Canadians, or is it going to take us five years under the Access to Information Act?

I have to fundamentally disagree with that. The goods and services tax does not hurt low and middle income Canadians. Those same people will be receiving a rebate cheque four times a year amounting to $275 per adult, $100 per child.
That is quite different from what was the case with the sales tax system that we inherited five years ago. In 1986 we introduced the notion of a rebate, a refundable sales tax credit. We have increased the size of that and the number of people who will receive that rebate by a large amount. In fact, the total amount of the rebate will be $3.6 billion.
That is a clear indication to Canadians that we are concerned about the impact of sales taxes on low-income people, but we are also acting to protect those same people.

Mr. Speaker, I remind the minister that even his back-benchers would disagree with him on this point. Is this government committed, through taxation of the poor, to make the food banks the fastest growing banking chain in this country?

Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member is concerned that the indexation is CPI minus three.
She should understand also that we have made a commitment to review this on an ongoing basis and adjust that low-income threshold as is appropriate. We started off the refundable sales tax credit with a low income threshold of $15,000, we increased it to $16,000, then to $18,000, and now with the GST proposal to $25,000. Surely she can understand that we are being responsive to the needs of the same people she is talking about.
Basic groceries are not under our proposal, that is food that is acquired by food banks, and will not be subject to

tax. Clearly, we have the interests of lower-income people in mind as we constructed this proposal.

We have penetrated that market because of our high quality and because of the demand.
If there is any issue that has to be contended with, it is the United States continued use of the export enhancement program and its non-commercial credit terms, which are very generous and which in effect distort the market-place in grains and oilseeds in the world.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council

That is a clear recognition of the fact that their subsidies are at a much higher level than ours. Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Last week, I asked the minister about the release of documents requested under the Access to Information Act which would show whether the Tory campaign promises were made in good faith.

Mr. Speaker, the advice that is rendered by a Deputy Minister flows back and forth as a result of discussions, consultations and a range of other matters that end up forming that advice. It does not matter whether it is on policy matters that relate to the economic policies of the government or other broader ranging policy matters, it still falls under the category of advice. As the hon. member knows, as a former minister, that is protected by the Access to Information Act for very obvious reasons.

It is very important that that free flow of information and advice between the minister and the deputy minister is maintained. That is the basis on which I have acted in relation to this particular access to information question.

Mr. Speaker, I think the House can only take it from that answer that the minister has indeed rejected the advice that he has received about what documents should be released.
Was his decision to reject advice about the interpretation of the Access to Information Act based on independent legal advice that he has obtained?
Mr. Speaker, here we are talking again about advice.
Legal advice.

Well, legal advice comes through the deputy minister through the departmental legal officers. This information is still by nature of advice, but clearly I am not going to be acting in ways that are totally counter to things that have been said to me in the department.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Loiselle that Bill C-20, an act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act, be read the third time and passed.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will not go to the next chapter of my book on "the grabbiest government in Canadian history".
I just want to continue to a certain extent with the impact of Bill C-20 on the more remote areas of the country. As I pointed out before, we have in place already a communication tax which discriminates against rural and remote areas of the country, a discrimination tax which will operate very much like the GST the government is proposing. Its impact will be much greater
in remote and rural areas than it will be in much of central Canada. That is part of the reason we think that the whole approach of Bill C-20 is probably the greatest tax grab of any Canadian government.
Another area of concern, particularly for Canadians in remote areas but for all Canadians to a certain extent, is the increase on building materials because that tax affects every area of the country. It affects those areas where the costs of building are already extremely high. Constructing of a building in the Northwest Territories will cost more per square foot and consequently you are going to pay a larger proportion of tax than someone building in the south or in a more densely populated area.
The increase of the tax from 8 per cent to the 9 per cent, which is provided in this particular bill, is not fair in the sense that it is a larger tax on people who are required to spend more than others on construction.
It is difficult to talk about this bill without talking about the impact of the GST as well. In the northern and rural areas the GST will be a tax on the final product and, since that final product is going to be much more expensive than it would be ordinarily in downtown Regina, for instance, it will cost those people more than other Canadians. In fact, if you look closely at the budget, you will find that because of a 40 per cent decrease in regional development all regions of the country except central Canada and the larger cities will be impacted negatively by this bill, by this tax, and by the policies of the government.
There are other things we should talk about with this bill besides its impact on northerners and rural people. This grab is going to have the greatest effect on middle income earners and in fact will have the opposite effect on large profit making corporations.
The government has been talking about the goods and services tax since before the budget. It made a lot of promises during the election period and following. For instance, it was going to eliminate the surtax. Now we are told it will not eliminate the surtax but will leave it in place. It is a tax which in itself is discriminatory because the surtax does not really mean very much to a large corporation with a good tax lawyer. If you end up paying no tax, as 60,000 corporations have indicated, an 8 per cent surtax on nothing is nothing. The impact of the surtax was minimal. They were told it would be taken off, and now it is going to be left on.
October 23, 1989

In addition, all Canadians are going to have to pay a surtax, particularly those who are on salary. There is no way. Regardless how good a tax lawyer they have, people on salary will find a loophole large enough not to pay any tax.
Also, the social programs are being attacked. A good example is the Unemployment Insurance Act which is being changed, worth a 15 per cent increase in premiums being paid. That is a 15 per cent increase that is being taken directly out of the salary of the workers who pay those premiums. The total effect of all these changes range from $700 to $1,700 a year. This is a major impact resulting in much less money that can be spent on keeping the economy going and flowing into the coffers of the government, where it seems to disappear while doing very little good for anybody at all.
Since this government has been in power taxes have increased by 171 per cent. That is a huge increase in taxes. With this bill the government is continuing in the same direction. That is why our party and the people of Canada believe that more time and effort should be put into establishing a fair taxation system which would tax those people who are able to pay and relieve those who find it difficult to pay even a small increase in taxes.

Mr. Speaker, I can think of some things that can be cut. One of them is the interest rate. If there was a one point decrease in interest rates, it would amount to $3 billion in the coffers of the government. That is the kind of cut that would be of some value to the government.
There are other things that can be done. One of them is to put in place a fair kind of taxation which collects, for instance, the $34 billion which the large corporations are holding as deferred taxes. Something that we have been suggesting for years is a minimum corporation tax. Even the Reagan government in the U.S. made some move in that direction by putting on a 20 per cent minimum corporation tax.
The large corporations have been able to escape paying any kind of tax by using the tax loopholes that are in place. The 20 per cent minimum tax would be there regardless of whether they were able to sneak through those loopholes. Those are the kinds of measures that will make the difference in bringing in the money by other means instead of cutting away from the social services and programs that people need and increasing taxation on the low and middle income Canadians who can least afford it.

Mr. Speaker, I was impressed by the member's comments just prior to the dinner adjournment when he was discussing how the goods and services tax would have a compounding impact on the high cost of living in northern Canada. This was brought home to me a couple of weeks ago when I went with one of my Liberal colleagues up to northern Quebec to talk to the Cree and Inuit communities there.
I found out that when you go a certain distance north in Quebec, you no longer get free access to the federal government telephone lines. For example, to contact Health and Welfare Canada or to find out about your pensions or family allowance cheques, you have to make a long distance toll call from northern Canada in order to deal with those departments of the national government to which you would have free access if you lived in southern Canada.
Now, in addition to the toll call, you are going to be obliged to pay the telecommunications tax under this Excise Tax Act. When the GST comes in, you are going to be required to pay a 9 per cent tax on the toll calls you make just to get federal services and advice from federal agencies that are free if you were living in the southern part of Canada. It shows the kind of compounding effect that this tax will have on the unfair treatment we give to northern communities. I appreciated the member's comments on that.

October 23, 1989
Government Orders
I was really surprised to hear the member for Abitibi, in whose riding I was a visitor, talk now about the air parcel staging rate that the government through the Canada Post Corporation has just increased by 32 per cent. This is a parcel delivery system in the north where Canada Post ships groceries and medications to northern communities that have no other means of getting those goods other than through air service or through the Canada Post system. This government has now increased those rates by 32 per cent. Furthermore, it has cut back on the subsidy that used to be available through Indian Affairs or through Industry, Science and Technology by about $1 million a year over the last year.
This government appears not to value northern Canada at all and discriminates especially against native communities in northern Canada. In this legislation we are seeing a government that wants to compound the cost of living in the north, compound the cost of living in native communities. It seems to provide no useful relief at all to those who live in the north at much higher rates than in the south.

Mr. Speaker, it is very interesting that the government has been saying for years-and we have agreed with it quite often-that the manufacturers' tax has some problems. You have doubled the tax that the consumer is going to pay on those items. That is true for every consumer item that is being taxed now. The manufacturers' tax was at the manufacturers' level. Now it will be at the final consumer level. A 4 per cent decrease is actually, almost, a 100 per cent increase in many cases.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a real privilege and honour to stand today and discuss Bill C-20, an act to amend the Excise Tax.
From the commencement of this session of Parliament we have been involved in debates over taxes, and the legacy continues. What we and the Canadian public are witnessing is an unparalleled part of Canadian history. What we are witnessing is the government parading through, bill after bill, legislation after legislation, cause after cause, with one thing in common-a continual increase in taxes, all sorts of taxes that are eating into the incomes of low and middle income Canadians.
How many times this session will we hear from the government that no one likes to pay taxes or taxes are not popular, or that it needs to raise taxes, because of the financial mess this country is in? When will the tax parade stop? Is it the intention of the this government to make tax grab the catch word of the 1990s?
I use the parade as a comparison as well. We in Canada look on parades as a group of floats and bands going by. This government has brought forth a float of taxes-tax, after tax, after tax-and stood on the bandstand telling Canadians how well they are doing. Let us look at this specific float known as Bill C-20.
Government Orders
Bill C-20 contains the necessary legislative amendments to implement the federal sales tax, excise tax and excise duty changes announced in the budget of April 27, 1989. Nice rhetoric. What it means to all Canadians is: hold on to your wallet, hold on to your purse, hold on to your cheque book, the tax grab continues. What it means is that cigarettes will cost more, gasoline will cost more, using your telephone will cost more, home construction and repairs will cost more, a drink will cost more, many manufactured goods in this country will cost more. Indeed an impressive offering. Almost everything you do, buy, or dream of will cost you more. The proposed tax increases in Bill C-20 will affect all Canadians. All Canadians will pay more for almost every purchase.
These increases will hurt low and middle income families more because of the percentage of income spent on necessities like housing for a family, for the gasoline used to drive to work. These taxes are not aimed at luxury items. These tax increases are aimed right at the heart of the consumer market, and the parade continues.
Last November the government stated that the economy of Canada was in good shape. It said its spending commitments made during the election campaign were not going to cost Canadians more. That was November 1988. In April 1989 the Minister of Finance introduced the federal budget that would reduce government programs by $2 billion and increase tax revenues by $5 billion. At the same time the government told us that the deficit reduction and public debt reduction were foremost in the government's mind. That was on its mind in November. What was there?
When the government told us everything was okay, what was the drastic change in five months? In May or June the parade of legislative tax proposals began and it continues today. Increase of sales, an increase here or higher excise tax there, a little more duty charged here, while by the way, making the average Canadian the brunt of that tax burden. The government, even with this legislation, will not simply say: "Here is the plan, pay up". No. The government tells us Bill C-20 is necessary as a revenue bridge to sales tax reform.
A revenue bridge is interesting terminology. It means let us get the tax and excise revenues hiked up very high so that the rest of its tax reform proposals, such as the GST, will not be so painful. At least, they will not appear so painful. How does this revenue bridge really work? Let us look at the goods and services tax proposal and the current manufacturers' sales tax.

Government Orders
In 1984 the manufacturers' sales tax was 9 per cent. By the time the 1989 budget rolled around, the Conservative government had it up to 13.5 per cent, an increase of 4.5 per cent in just five years. Talk about revenue bridge, this is a revenue rocket.
If inflation on average is 5 per cent per year for the last five years, and the current manufacturers' sales tax is 13.5 per cent and is used to raise $18.5 billion, then in 1984-85 terms, the manufacturers' sales tax would have raised less than $10 billion. It would appear that the manufacturers' sales tax, raising less than $10 billion in 1984 and raising $18.5 billion in 1990 and having its rate go up from 9 per cent in 1984 to 13.5 per cent in 1989 is being used as far more than just a temporary revenue bridge. The tax is being used by this government to generate almost twice as much money today as it did five years ago. The problems attributed to the MST by this government have been compounded by its own initiatives.
The finance minister has called the MST a silent killer of jobs. Little wonder when you consider the rate has gone up 50 per cent and the revenues have doubled since 1984. The government has created a monster with which it must now deal. How does it choose to deal with it? Simple, call it a killer. Blame past governments and make Canadians pay for it, then introduce a new tax. Sell Canadians on it. Call it revenue neutral, but generate another $5.5 billion in taxes for Canadians. The average Canadian pays again.
I love a parade, but this parade has to stop. Bill C-20 will do the following; increase federal sales taxes on construction material from 8 per cent to 9 per cent, increase alcohol and tobacco taxes from 18 per cent to 19 per cent, increase the manufacturers' sales tax from 12 per cent to 13.5 per cent, increase telecommunications services from 10 per cent to 11 per cent, increase the excise tax on gasoline by one cent a litre as of March, 1989, another one cent a litre in January, 1990, plus an additional one cent a litre on leaded fuels, increase excise taxes and duties on tobacco products by $4 per carton of cigarettes and a similar amount on cigars, and place a $5.30 levy on a 200-gram container of manufactured tobacco.
The estimated take on the excise taxes and duties alone is $.9 billion in 1984 and has been increased to $1.6 billion by 1990. That increase again is $.9 billion from 1984 to $1.6 billion in 1990.
While the bill proposes increased tax credits and raising income thresholds from $16,000 to $18,000 in 1990, Canadians will not maintain their purchasing power. Farmers, for example, will lose their farm fuel rebate program. In my riding of Essex-Kent, farmers will pay more for such things as fuel by 1990 than they do today. This holds true for farmers everywhere in Canada.
Today, fuel rebates are 8.5 cents a litre and 7.5 cents a litre for diesel fuel. Yet in 1990, the rebate will be reduced to 3.5 cents per litre and by 1991, if the government has its own way, the rebate would be, based on the GST, reduced to 2.8 cents a litre, more than 5.5 cents per litre reduction in just two years, or two-thirds of that rebate being reduced.
The government claims a savings here of $200 million. What type of saving is this? How is this a saving if actual costs are just foisted on the already beleaguered agricultural community? A fault savings indeed. Yet, the government claims that these are necessary legislative amendments, that they are necessary to implement the federal sales tax, the excise tax and the excise duty changes that will provide a revenue bridge to the sales tax reform, a reform that is regressive, discriminatory, ill-conceived, and impossible to nurture. It is a tax that the members opposite would have us all sit back and enjoy while we sacrifice segments of the Canadian economy that can ill afford such expensive initiatives.
Bill C-20, in many respects is a forerunner of the government's proposed goods and services tax. The government needs the legislative changes proposed in Bill C-20 to pave its way for the introduction of the new GST. Is it not odd that we are reviewing legislation to make it easier to introduce a GST that has not yet been considered by this House? Is it not odd that Bill C-20 lays the groundwork for legislation which, although in draft form, has not been finally prepared? The GST legislation may receive wholesale revision at the committee stage before final consideration, or, more preferable, if the government were truly tuned to Canadians, the GST would be scrapped altogether and not introduced at all.
October 23, 1989

Is it not strange that we are hastily arranging legislation now for something yet to happen, if it happens at all? That is all a part of the tax parade, a parade that will have us muddle through a myriad of legislation, a tax reform prerequisite before the real crunch is brought in.
Today, one-fifth of Canadian youth, about 1.2 million live below the poverty line. Today, the National Council of Welfare states that current pension plans do not meet the needs of seniors with over 600,000 seniors living below the poverty line. Today, financing costs in Canada are higher on average, between 3 per cent and 4 per cent, than their U.S. counterparts. Today, inflation in our country has risen by .5 per cent to 1 per cent in the second quarter of 1989 due directly to today's tax initiatives by the government. Today, the government continues to increase taxes that will be a direct assault on Canada, its youth, seniors, businesses and farmers. Is this the type of government that we can afford? What does Bill C-20 do to alleviate the burden on these people? Nothing. It does nothing. Enjoy the parade.
Where does the bill really lead us? It leads us further and further along the tax reform road, a road that has as its ultimate destination the GST, a tax reform that has partially indexed thresholds and credits, a tax reform that is hidden, a tax reform that is regressive and discriminatory, a tax reform that will strangle our economy, have taxes rise at a rate higher than inflation, cause more and more Canadians to lose their tax credits, remove billions of dollars from disposable incomes and investment incomes and sacrifice thousands of Canadian jobs. The tax reform which commences with Bill C-20 will have devastating consequences.
The government's parade of tax legislation will not stop until it is all in place. It is a tax reform that does not address the issues of the homeless, farm stabilization, lower interest rates and the protection of universal social benefits. This is no tax reform. It is just a parade.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak in strong opposition to Bill C-20, an act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act.
Government Orders
This bill is a result of tax changes that were announced in the recent federal budget. This bill provides for increases in the manufacturers' sales tax from 12 per cent to 13.5 per cent and a tax on cigarettes and gasoline.
I rise to speak on behalf of my constituents in Haldimand-Norfolk, especially those in the tobacco industry who have been hard hit by this government's taxation policy. Once again, this government is attempting to reduce the deficit through heavy tax increases which hit middle and lower-income Canadians the hardest.
The manufacturers' sales tax is a regressive tax that impacts more on lower income Canadians than it does on the more affluent. As we have heard many times in this House during this debate and other debates, the Minister of Finance himself has referred to this tax as the silent killer of jobs. I can agree with that.
The budget was an ominous one. The Prime Minister promised tax fairness. The Minister of Finance's budget proposals made massive increases in personal taxes while corporate taxes continued to decline.
Since 1984 the average-income Canadian family is now paying an extra $2,000 in taxes as a result of the finance minister's budget. I ask the government, is this a progressive tax when Canadians have had to pay over $2,000 more in taxes since this government has come into power?
A progressive tax system means you pay taxes according to your ability to pay. This helps reduce inequality and helps raise the standard of living on the bottom end of the income scale. This is not being done at all through these tax increases. A regressive tax is one which makes the poor pay a higher percentage of their income in tax. This is what the Conservative government is doing to the poor.
Let me address the issue of agriculture because, as you know, Haldimand-Norfolk is one of the finest agriculture constituencies in this country. This regressive excise tax without a doubt will have an adverse effect on the people and on the agriculture and farming in my riding.
According to 1986 statistics, 20 per cent of the people of my riding depend on agriculture for employment. I strongly believe that this government is trying to get out of direct support for the family farm as a centrepiece of Canadian agriculture. The drive to incorporate farming accelerates the decline of rural communities. The small towns depend on and are affected greatly by this government's tax measures.

October 23, 1989
Government Orders
High interest rates devastate net farm income. Farm debt must be restructured to ensure the continued survival of the family farm. Debt write-down is necessary. The budget outlined a number of drastic cuts to agriculture programs which will have a devastating effect on farmers, especially those in my riding such as tobacco farmers, daily farmers and grain farmers.
Let us look briefly at some of the budget cuts this government has decided to implement. I believe that we have to look at the whole system. We have to look not only at what programs this government is providing to farmers but we also have to look at what is cut, especially in this last budget.
In the Crop Insurance Cost Sharing Program, the federal government will be cutting down from $90 million to $110 million its share in the next two years by rebalancing of the cost. Producers, suggesting a one-third tripartite funding proposal, were squarely rejected by this government. Without an equitable funding mechanism such as the crop insurance premium cost, it will remain too expensive for many growers, especially in the poorer provinces. This means a continuation of low participation percentages among producers of many farm commodities.
Without a high participation percentage the economic and political need for ad hoc disaster relief programs will continue just as it has in the past.
Of course, we all know about the removal of the interest free provision to the Advance Payments for Crops Act under Bill C-36, which we debated earlier last week in this House. Farm organizations and members of our party have strongly opposed this legislation, but in doing so have been accused of depriving farmers of advance payments for the 1989 crop year. We called upon this government to withdraw that bill. Unfortunately it is still pressing on but we will continue to fight it. In reality, the present act authorizes such payments and only reluctance by this minister to exercise authority spelled out in the existing legislation prevents funds from now being disbursed to producers across this country. I do not like to say that the minister directly misled this House but he directly told farmers something that was not true.
We have asked this government to withdraw this legislation and to allow consultation on this matter. Unfortunately, this government does not have the insight to see the negative impact of this bill on agriculture. It is obvious that this government's strength does not he in insight or understanding. Perhaps I am being too kind. Perhaps it does understand the negative impact of its so-called progressive changes and it just does not care. It has to be one or the other, and I am not quite sure which it is.
Coming from an agricultural riding, I am naturally concerned about the increased excise tax, and how this will affect farmer's actual cost of production. It has been estimated that the cumulative effects of the tax and the rebate changes will have very negative impacts on our agricultural industries. For example, the budget stated that leaded gasoline would increase by 2 cents a litre April 28, 1989, and as a result of federal sales tax, it would increase by a further .39 of a cent per litre June 11, 1989. The federal excise tax is to increase again on January 1, 1990, by one whole cent. On top of all this, the federal fuel rebate of 5 cents per litre will be eliminated effective January 1, 1990.
It does not take a rocket scientist to know that farmers, especially farmers in my area of Haldimand-Norfolk, will be affected greatly by this. The cumulative fuel cost increase to farmers works out to be 8.39 cents per litre between April 1, 1989, and January 1, 1990. That is 8 cents a litre. Can you imagine going to the gas pump and finding that your gas has gone up 8.39 cents a litre?

speechtext: Shame!

The member is right, it is shameful. We call on this government to do something about it.
Similarly, product prices for unleaded gasoline will increase by 7.1 cents while diesel will climb by 4.32 cents. This government says that we should bring down the deficit. Why is it bringing this deficit down on the backs of Canadian farmers, on the backs of those people who can least afford to pay?
Estimates by the Ontario Federation of Agriculture, based on Statistics Canada data, put the additional cost to farmers of the fuel tax rebate changes to Ontario at more than $25 million. This is just for Ontario farmers. As you can see, we are not talking about small pennies here.
October 23, 1989

A spokesman for the Canadian Tobacco Manufacturing Council has said that the increases are abusive, inflationary, regressive, and counter-productive. I could not say it any better myself. Farmers are telling this to this minister. The poor who are heaviest per capita smokers will be hardest hit by these measures. The new taxes come four months after the federal government banned most forms of tobacco advertising.
Mr. A1 Bow, vice-chairman of the Ontario Flue-cured Tobacco Growers Marketing Board has indicated: "I don't know if we can recover this time". This is somewhat surprising because this Minister of Agriculture came to my riding and said: "Ottawa wants to send a strong signal to the industry that we are here to support tobacco producers in their time of need and in their time of adjustment". My colleagues know when he said that. He said that during the election campaign. Sure enough, after the election campaign he tells tobacco farmers, "Yes, we are going to support you but we are going to tax the heck out of you. We are not only going to tax you on the top end by taxing cigarettes, we are also going to tax your fuel. We are also going to increase your cost of production." That to me does not seem like support for our agricultural community. The government estimates reveal that there will be an increase of over $6 million in 1989-90 in assistance towards the orderly diversification of the tobacco-producing industry. This is a program set up to help tobacco farmers adjust into other farming sectors because of the conditions brought upon the industry by this government's adverse taxing policies. You would think that if you are asking tobacco farmers to move into other areas of production, and if you are going to over tax them, you would use some of that money on the bottom end to help them move into other crops. What the government has done is it cut out that program. It has slashed it.
What they have done is they have cut that out, slashed it. The government is telling tobacco farmers that it wants them to get out of the industry but it does not want to help them get out, they are going to have to find then-own way out.
Government Orders
This government takes billions and billions of dollars out of tobacco each year. Surely it could put a little of that money back into the industry.
Why is it that this government promises one thing before an election and immediately afterwards goes back on its word? How can anyone trust this government? It is obvious that Canadians can no longer trust this government's word. If it promises one thing to farmers, it should stand by that promise. Farmers expect this, as do all Canadians.
It is this government's policies that have put the agriculture industry into the fragile position it is in today. A great deal of that has to do with this government's policies. Let us for a minute take another look at another promise.
During the free trade debate, this government promised Canadian farmers that they would have total access to the American markets. The Minister of Agriculture came into my riding and told dairy farmers that supply management would be protected by this government. Right in my own riding, he told the pork farmers that the Americans would stop harassing them, now that we had this free trade agreement we did not have to worry about American harassment.

speechtext: It is a fraud.

speechtext:
That is right, it is a fraud because, quite frankly, Canadian farmers want this government to live up to its words, stand up and tell the Americans, "We are not going to take this any more".
We have seen since free trade, and since the election was over, Americans harassing us on steel, pork, ice cream, yogurt and fishing. How can any agriculturalist believe the word of this government? The people believed the word of the government during the last election. They said, "Sure, we are going to give up all these things under free trade, but look what we are going to get in return. We are not going to get harassment". Well, we have seen over the past few months exactly what has happened and how good this government's word is.
Actions by this government clearly show that it does do not give two cents about agriculture. In fact, the quicker it can destroy the industry, the better.

Government Orders
This government is one of total regression. It is exemplified in the proposed goods and services tax. This ominous legislation is on the lips and minds of people from all walks of life. I had the opportunity during the past month to go to two fall fairs in my riding. Fall fairs are places where you can see thousands and thousands of people. Last year, the fairs were held during the election campaign so it was a good opportunity for us in rural Canada to sit down and talk to individual Canadian constituents.
I had some petitions on the side of my booth and quite frankly, we had to have a police officer to direct traffic because there were so many people signing petitions. The petition called upon this government to get rid of the goods and services tax. Thousands of my constituents, as have the constituents of my colleagues on this side of the House, were signing petitions. I am sure that if we have had thousands of petitioners, there must be thousands from the other side of the House calling upon this government to get rid of this tax.
This is just one adverse way that this government continues in its bad taxation policies. Time after time before the House of Commons committee looking into this issue, witnesses have appeared warning the government that this proposed tax is flawed and unworkable. Does this government listen? No, it does not, not any more than it listened to us when we warned it not to rush into signing the free trade agreement. You can see the commonality between the two issues. The government did not listen then and now we regularly find ourselves being challenged by the United States.
Raising $9 billion to combat the burgeoning deficit is not a mean feat for any finance minister, especially when this government has doubled the national debt in four years.
We saw in the newspaper today figures that show this government's deficit has increased another few billion dollars. It seems that when this government gives a projection as to what the budget deficit will be, it is always off by a billion or two. I do not understand. I think it takes a little common sense to know that if you bring down interest rates, the deficit will also come down.
This government's policy on interest rates is flawed. If the Conservatives would listen to the Canadian people, they would let them know that in fact it is a flawed program. Unfortunately, the only way to lower the deficit, from the government's point of view, is to reverse fundamental policy positions from its election campaign. We have seen that throughout this session.
I am unsure of my time, Mr. Speaker. I have three more minutes, thank you.
Over the last five years, this government has gone to great lengths to blatantly insist that its tax measures have been part of a master plan to broaden the tax base, lower income tax rates, eliminate special preferences and curb opportunities for tax avoidance. This is what the government says. This government has exhausted its tax grab opportunities on personal income tax. Now it is going for a tax on consumption.
Canadians are getting wiser. Some taxpayers, notably small entrepreneurs, are starting to realize that they cannot afford to rush too enthusiastically after tax and other incentives offered by this government because, quite frankly, they cannot believe them. Specific measures introduced in previous years to encourage investment in certain types of activities or in certain regions of the country have been limited or removed altogether.
Over the years, several programs to encourage individual taxpayers to invest in scientific research were gutted. This government stressed and continues to stress that research and development is vital for the growth and competitiveness of our businesses, but it has cut all the programs. This is just another example of how it is hard for Canadians to believe what this government says.
Sales tax reform is heralded as an improvement to the fairness of the tax system by allowing the application of lower rates to a much broader tax base. However, this $1 billion tax grab is highly regressive despite the proposed tax credit system for lower income taxpayers.
We also saw in the paper recently a study done by the Globe and the CBC, I believe. The study said that 80 per cent of Canadians were against this tax. Surely, the government can see the ill of its ways in trying to bring in this tax reform. Canadians clearly do not agree with this.
I see my time is almost up. I want to leave by reiterating what I said about the effects of this tax on agriculture. Farmers in my area told me clearly, and I am sure all the members on the other side have been told, that they do not mind paying their fair share of taxes, but they are sick and tired of being the ones who are always taxed. They do not want this tax. They are the whipping boys of this government and, quite frankly, they are not prepared to stand idly by this time. They are prepared to stand up and let this government know that it is not doing the right thing. They told me that next election it will be this side for whom they will be voting.
October 23, 1989

I want to go one step further and congratulate the people of his riding who, notwithstanding the fact that the minister came during the election campaign and made an appeal to the people of his riding, they had the good foresight to elect my friend to represent them in the House of Commons, and a fine job he is doing.

It is interesting, talking about cleaning, that this bill intends to increase the wholesale tax on laundiy detergent. Mr. Speaker, I flipped through Bill C-20 which I will be speaking on today to see what is in the bill. It seemed like a rather innocuous title, an act to Amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act. But when I looked in the contents, I found sort of a wolf in sheep's clothing. The government was trying to trick us, I would suggest, into believing that it is something without very many teeth, that it is something very quiet with no problems for the people of Canada.
But when you look a little deeper, it is clear that this particular bill is part of the agenda that we have seen under this present government since 1984, a constant tax grab from the lower and middle income people of Canada. We look at what is in the bill and we see that it contains a tax on telecommunications. Well, on the surface that does not seem so very serious. People who use telecommunications are probably large corporations and they are going to be taxed. But if we look at who this is affecting, we find out that the people in the Northwest Territories and the people in the Yukon are the ones using telecommunications constantly to keep in touch with their relatives in the rest of Canada and the United States. The telecommunications tax is going to hit people in the far regions, in the Atlantic Provinces, in the west, including British Columbia where I come from. Often people in these regions, particularly in the north, have come from areas such as Ontario, southern British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Central Ontario and they want to keep in touch with their friends and relatives. With this particular bill the government has, in fact, taxed the person who has moved out of those areas and is populating our frontier areas, areas to which we must look for our future growth. They are being hit, I would submit, by this telecommunications tax.
I looked further to see what else the government has hit. It has taxed gasoline. If we look at the environmental aspect of that, it is not such a bad deal because the environmental argument is that it discourages the use of fossil fuels. But let's face it, here in Canada where we have such a broad area to cover, where we have miles and miles between communities, between families, it is not, I would submit, a luxury to be able to drive a vehicle from the outer areas into town for groceries. Sometimes, particularly up north, that requires miles and miles of driving, but they are the people who we are hitting with this tax. It is not a luxury tax, it is an essential part of living, an essential part of life.
October 23, 1989

It is unfortunate that the government cannot see that by adding the excise tax on gasoline it is hitting families, it is hitting the poor, it is hitting those on fixed incomes. Although from an environmental point of view the increased excise tax on leaded fuels is a desirable thing, many people across Canada who are among our poverty-stricken, among those who are on fixed incomes, cannot afford cars that use unleaded gasoline. They have the old beaters, the old pick-up trucks from prior to 1978. Those are the types of vehicles they must purchase to get their families around, to go in to town to get groceries and the very necessities of life. As well, perhaps they have to take a spouse to the hospital for an operation, and so on. They are the people who are going to be hit with this tax. It is a tax again on the poor.
The tax on cigarettes and liquor I really have very little argument with. I feel those are things that Canadians can do without. It, in fact, is similar to a luxury tax. I cannot object to that.
But I look over the last few years since 1984 to find out what has happened to the taxes. I see that corporate taxes are down a percentage point from 13 to 12 per cent. I see that upper-income earners' tax has dropped from 34 per cent to 29 per cent. I look at the other side of the ledger to see what has increased. We have increased all of these taxes I have just spoken about. But, in addition, since 1984 we have increased the manufacturers' sales tax from 9 per cent to the present 13.5 per cent. Building materials under this bill would go up to 9 per cent from 8 per cent. What effect is that going to have? On the manufacturers' sales tax end of it, there will be a 1.5 per cent increase from the 12 per cent it is at present, up 3 per cent from what it was in 1984. We have had three consecutive increases in the manufacturers' sales tax since 1984.
Who does that hurt? Where does it hit? Again, it is a consumption-style tax. It hits the poor. It hits those on fixed incomes, those in the middle-income groups. The people who can least afford to pay are the ones who are hit by these consumption taxes.

11.5	per cent of the incomes of families earning $10,000 or less; 6.7 per cent of the incomes of families earning $40,000; but only 4.4 per cent of the income of families earning $100,000.1 wonder, is this fair?
