We have seen this constant agenda of turning more and more to consumption taxes. The government now argues that the manufacturers' sales tax is not fair, that it is a silent killer of jobs and we have to do away with it. It is now 13.5 per cent so the government will make it 9 per cent.
However, the government does not tell us that the
13.5	per cent, of course, is on the manufacturers' level and as everybody in the chain up to the retail level takes his piece of the action that 13.5 per cent does not increase. However, with the value added concept that we are now getting into, at each stage we are adding the 9 per cent onto the value that we have added to the price of the good. So a $100 good out of the manufacturer would normally bring in $13.50 in tax. By the time it gets to the retail level it has increased to $200. By my multiplication, we will now pay $18 in tax instead of $13.50. But that is not what this government has told the people of Canada. It has said it was going to be a smaller tax. The issue, I would suggest, is not whether we should have a value added tax, which in this case we are calling a goods and services tax, but whether Canada can afford to have a value added tax.

In one of the finance committee hearings we listened to a group called the Tax Executive Institute and we questioned the members of the group about what was happening. This group was made up of 80 per cent U.S. tax executives along with a vice-president to talk to us about a value added tax. We asked the vice-president what the Americans have done in the area of a value added tax; how far it had ever gone. It has been tried a few times, we were told, but unsuccessfully. It won't float past the first stages of discussion. Why? Because this is a tax that will be almost impossible to administer, the complexity of implementation will be enormous.
Within their own group of tax executives they could not get agreement that a value added tax was the route to go. Yet, in Canada, although we are tying our kite to the string of the United States and trying to fly everything that they fly, we are going to try a value added tax that is unlikely to come into the United States in the foreseeable future, and I would suggest probably not for at least 20 years down the road or perhaps never. Yet, here in Canada we are going to try it, but we are going to try it in a manner that has never been tried in the world before; we are going to use a two-tiered system. We have a provincial tax, but we are not going to go with the provinces, we are going to try it on our own federally. So we are going to make it totally impossible for those out there who are gathering it to bring this in.
That is a problem with what we have done, but the problem is the tax itself. It is a regressive tax. It hurts the poor, the middle income earners, and those on fixed incomes such as the old age pensioners. It is not the answer to what we in Canada need for the future.
I looked at some of the problems with some of the witnesses who have appeared before the finance committee hearings on the technical paper. We have talked to farmers and the farmers tell us they do not want this tax. If we have to bring it in then they need certain exclusions. But the basic message is that a value added tax is going to hurt everybody up the line in administration.
We talk of the input credits and the government says, "Well, it does not really matter because you are a farmer and you are going to get back all of your input credits". I wonder where those people in their little ivory towers have been all their lives because they sure as heck have not been out on the farms talking to the farmers. They have not been in the small businesses talking to the business people. Those are the people who have to administer this.
You hear the bureaucrats in the Department of Finance, who have written this technical paper, telling us it is going to be simple, it is going to be easy to administer. It is so simple, you simply take the tax and you take your input credits and you subtract and you add and you send away this money and you get it all back. Nonsense! The people who have to do it are frightened to death of this administrative nightmare that the government has put them in.
They have bookkeeping problems. We talked to a potato farmer in Prince Edward Island. He said, "Look, I work from dawn until dusk. Although I run a farm with 1,100 acres of potatoes, my wife and I still do our own bookkeeping. Even though we may go out and spend $100,000 a year on equipment, we do not have the time to fill in the paper to get back our rebate".
A lot of farmers tell us they are not computerized, as are a lot of small businesses. So what happens? The farmers tell us that a lot of them will not be getting back the input credits, so it is simply going to cost them the 9 per cent more. I say that this is shameful. This is only one example of what is happening under the goods and services tax.
One of the other examples, is in the area of the poor. Government members on the committee constantly tell us, "Well, we have worked in this nice tax credit system, rebates for those with incomes under $24,000". Well that is all well and good. Go up to the Northwest Territories or the Yukon where they tell us that the illiteracy rate is higher than anywhere else in Canada. The trappers out on the traplines live a subsistence living I am told. They do not file income tax returns. They know nothing about tax credits. But, in order to run their traplines they buy snowmobiles, gasoline and their traps, and they have to pay the tax on top of that. They are not going to get any of their rebates back. It is simply going to cost those people more and they are already paying 25 per cent more for all of their goods and services than we, down in the southern regions, are paying. So it is a double taxation on those from the outer regions.

I, for one, think that most Canadians respect the fact that it is the government's responsibility, its duty, to make sure that we handle the economic affairs of this country in a proper and productive way. I do not believe that Canadians really begrudge the government attempting to do its job. I think what people were looking for, and I think what people trusted during the last election, was that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance when they approached tax reform would approach it in a more comprehensive way. People have such a frustration with the tax act and the tax system in general right now that there is a mood in the country that is providing a lot of disincentive. There is a disincentive to our entrepreneurs who want to be free to create and utilize their energy in making products that will, in turn, create jobs for Canadians. These products have to be made at such a level of quality and productivity that we are world class competitive. Just as we were coming out of the tough years of 1982 to 1984 and heading into a period when the economy was starting to really move again in 1985 to 1988, there was a sense of hope held by the entrepreneurs and many others in this country that we were finally going to put ourselves back on track.
What we have done with this tax system is shackle the entrepreneurs. We have provided a tremendous frustration level. I do not just point to entrepreneurs. Seniors citizens come to my constituency office. They do not know where to begin when they have 45 pages of rules and regulations and they try to figure out the tax system we have in this country. The frustration is just absolutely incredible. I know Revenue Canada does provide some service during peak periods, but this government should

be approaching tax reform in a comprehensive way. It has not had the courage to do so.

Just because you have the majority vote does not mean you have to continue with blind arrogance. It is not right.
We have to get a style and a system going in government where once we realize that we are doing something that is incorrect we fix it. We have the courage to fix it.
I think Canadians want their government to come up with a responsible plan. They want an end to the 50,000 pages that comprise the tax act. I do not think this feeling is unique to any one region, sector or social group. I think it is all Canadians. They want us to come forward with a system as the Minister of Finance promised in 1985, 1986 and 1988, which is more fair, simple, efficient and workable. If the Minister of Finance and the Government of Canada came up with a system like that we could reignite our economy.

The Minister of State for Finance said: "The additional revenue raised through these measures, the measures to amend the excise tax, are estimated at $2 billion in the first full year". The thing that I did not hear him deal with was the inflation factor of 2.5 per cent. If we went along with the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, we would see it estimates 5 per cent. We are talking about an extra three or four percentage points on the interest rate. That could be an added cost to the deficit of as much as $4 billion to $5 billion.
I stand to be corrected on that. But I know one thing. The $2 billion in revenue will virtually be eliminated for sure. It will be eliminated by the interest rate differential because of the increase in inflation.
My hon. friend from Halton-Peel shakes his head "no". He is a respected business commentator and now a member of Parliament for whom I have great feeling. If I am not accurate in that, I stand to be corrected, but I would like a thorough explanation on that. I have talked to economists and bankers. They are afraid that the inflationary effect of the GST is going to really affect our investment climate from abroad. That investment climate, once it is affected, will have an effect on our interest rate. Even now the Minister of Finance does not really have a will strong enough to give a direction to the Governor of the Bank of Canada. I presume that the reason why he is not doing that is because he is naturally concerned about inflation.
If he is concerned about inflation with the current interest rate, then why would it not be logical with an added inflation rate, because of this complicated tax system, that it would also affect our interest rates? That is the point that I am trying to make.
At any rate, I think that all too often in this House we forget about the disincentive factor. We are through Bill C-20 and the goods and services tax demoralizing our nation. I know that because I hear from people all the time. I will give just one short story.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
I would like to tell one final story, Mr. Speaker.
Last weekend I met a man who was in the marble tile business. His business was doing well. But his problem was that he could not find quality trained people who would work on weekends because of the disincentive factor of the tax system. People are saying: "I work all weekend but I end up keeping only 30 per cent to 40 per cent in my pocket". That is what I mean by the disincentive factor. I think it is time that we look at that when we approach this tax system. I think it is time that the government go back to the drawing board and worry about turning on the nation rather than turning it off.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to respond a little to the hon. member's views on interest rates. I will do it very quickly.
I know that the member has done a great deal of work on the issue of tax reform and I salute him on that. The issue of the inflationary effect of the proposed tax and the response to it by the Bank of Canada needs to be more than a knee-jerk one.
The Bank of Canada Governor has appeared before a parliamentary committee. He has said that he understands the threat of having higher interest rates responding to any GST induced inflation. He has told the parliamentary committee that he will not respond to GST induced inflation by jacking up interest rates. So we have some assurance from the Governor of the Bank of Canada himself on that.
We all recognize the real threat posed to the government's long term ability to manage the debt that is posed by interest rates. I agree with the hon. member on that very real threat. The only way we can get lower interest rates in the long term is to address the debt problem. Simply lowering rates to accomplish that is a very facile solution.
